activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In 1824 German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past 'as it actually was', rather than to judge it or instruct the present.
story:
Christopher had thirty-one hours to finish his history essay, and the question on the assignment sheet was the problem: "Can historians describe the past without judging it?" He spread his books across the library table by the window, three of them, plus a printout of a primary source he had found in the school database, and started with the book that seemed most promising.

The first book opened with a claim he copied onto an index card: in 1824 the German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past "as it actually was," rather than to judge it or instruct the present. Christopher liked the sound of that. It felt clean, like a photograph instead of an argument. He underlined the sentence twice, wrote RANKE at the top of the card, and set it beside his laptop.

Catherine dropped her bag on the chair across from him and stole a rice cake from his lunch. "You look like the books are winning," she said.

"I don't know what my thesis is." He turned the card so she could read it. "This guy says you can just show what happened. No judging, no lessons."

"So what's the problem?"

He pushed the printout toward her. It was a mill owner's letter from the same period Ranke had studied, describing his workers as content and well fed. Below it lay a page from the second book, a parliamentary report quoting a doctor who had inspected the same mills and found children with bent legs and coughs that never cleared. "Both of these are sources," Christopher said. "Both are from people who were actually there. The owner isn't lying exactly. He believes it. The doctor isn't lying either."

Catherine chewed and read. "So which one is 'as it actually was'?"

"Both. Or neither. That's the problem." He took the card back and looked at the underlined sentence again, and for the first time it seemed less like a photograph and more like a wish. Ranke had wanted to stand outside the past and point at it, but every source Christopher had was written by someone standing somewhere, looking at something from an angle. The owner's letter was partial because the owner saw what he wanted to see and wrote for an audience of other owners. The doctor's report was partial too; he had been sent to find sickness, so he found it, and left out the workers he passed in the corridor who seemed fine. Neither document was the past. Both were one person's piece of it.

He spent an hour testing the idea against the third book, which was garrulous in a way that was almost useful; its author never stopped talking, so every gap in the older sources got filled with a guess, and the guesses were marked clearly as guesses. Christopher began to see that the book's honesty was not in what it knew but in what it admitted it didn't. There was even a section in the back called a historiographical essay, tracing how historians had argued about the mills for a century, each generation asking different questions, one caring about production, one about wages, one about the workers' own accounts, which had mostly gone unrecorded until someone thought to look.

Mr. Nwosu, who taught down the hall and used the library on his free period, passed their table on his way to the periodicals and paused at the stack of books. "Mills?" he said, tapping the parliamentary report. "Brutal topic. There's a nice argument hiding in there." He kept walking before Christopher could ask what the argument was, which was typical, and which forced Christopher to find it himself.

He opened a new document and typed fast, before the sentence could dissolve. Ranke's aim, he wrote, might still be worth holding even if it was impossible to reach, because the alternative was letting the past be whatever you needed it to be; the point was to gather the partial pieces, say plainly which pieces were missing, and admit where the sources disagreed instead of smoothing it over. The essay would not show the mills as they actually were. It would show what remained of them, which was a different and smaller thing, but a true one. He read the opening line to Catherine: "The owner's letter and the doctor's report cannot both be the whole truth, and the historian who picks one and hides the other has not described the past but replaced it."

Catherine finished the last rice cake and slid the printout back across the table. "You should end with the two sources side by side," she said. "Just show them. Let the reader sit in it."

Christopher set the letter and the report next to each other on the table, the owner's tidy script above the doctor's cramped list of symptoms, and turned on the recorder app on his phone, reading both aloud into the quiet of the library, one after the other, without a word between them.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
story:
The clipboard said she had signed in at nine, which meant Alicia had been carrying a crate of kale for forty minutes before anyone asked her name. A man in a volunteer shirt, older, with soil under his fingernails, handed her a trowel and pointed to the bed nearest the fence. Behind him, the food bank's tables ran in rows down the church hall, and through the open doors she could see the community garden where the kale had grown, half of it already stripped for the morning pickup.

She had not wanted to come. Her mother had printed the form, circled the forty hours, and left it on the counter without comment, which was its own kind of comment. Ontario wanted forty hours of community involvement before it would hand her the diploma, and forty hours was a number that looked small until you tried to spend it. Mathys had finished his hours in grade nine, all at once, at a library shelving books he was not allowed to read on shift. He called it efficient. Alicia had called it something else at the time, a word she now regretted, because here she was in October of grade twelve, logging hours before a deadline like everyone she had pitied.

"You're the new one," said a girl at the next bed, pulling carrots. "Paolo. Well, I'm Paolo." He had a lanyard with a laminated sheet of paper reading HOURS TRACKER, and beneath that a tally drawn in marker that went past forty and kept going.

"I thought you'd stop at forty," Alicia said.

"At forty they give you the diploma. After that you just keep coming." He said it lightly, the way people say things they have decided not to make strange.

A woman in rubber boots crossed the garden with a bucket, and when she reached them she asked whether Alicia had logged her morning. This was Ms. Xu, who ran the garden and, it turned out, half the food bank's produce. Ms. Xu did not smile when she said that she did not sign the sheets until the student had done something worth signing, and she said it while looking at the kale bed, so that the sentence landed on the weeds in it. Alicia spent the next hour on her knees. The work was not difficult, only repetitive in a way that emptied her head, and she found she liked the emptiness, the smell of cut stems, the small clean line of turned soil behind her trowel.

At noon they moved crates inside. Paolo stacked cans and talked about a student council proposal to make volunteering mandatory beyond the requirement, an argument he found funny. "You can't mandate virtue," he said. "You can only mandate attendance." Alicia demurred; she thought some of the students at her school would never come at all unless something pushed them, and being pushed was how she had arrived here herself. He shrugged and kept stacking. It was not a fight, only the kind of exchange two people have while lifting things, each holding a position like a box, setting it down, picking it back up.

Inside, an older volunteer was sorting bread with a printed schedule taped above her station, and beside it a poster from some civic campaign about service that looked, in the church hall's fluorescent light, faintly anachronistic, all raised fists and wheat. Mathys had once argued in class that a state requiring service was drifting toward something like a theocracy of good deeds, where virtue became law and doubt became sin. Alicia had thought the phrase was clever. Now, watching a woman count loaves into bags for people who would line up at one o'clock, she thought the phrase was clever and also useless, the way most clever phrases were useless at a folding table with bread on it. Both things were true. Mathys was right that obligation could hollow out meaning; the woman with the bread was right that bread got bagged either way. Alicia could not make the two positions shake hands, and she noticed that she did not much want to.

Ms. Xu signed her sheet at the end of the shift. Four hours. Then she asked, not looking up, whether Alicia would be back Saturday, because the carrots would need pulling and Paolo's tally was the only reason the bed got done on time. Alicia said yes before she had decided to, and heard herself say it, and let it stand.

She walked to the bus stop with the signed sheet folded in her pocket, thirty-six hours from the diploma, and took out her phone to text Mathys that she had found a place he might actually like. Halfway through typing it she stopped, reread it, deleted it, and sent the sheet's photo to her mother instead. Then she got on the bus, and a man across the aisle looked at her muddy knees and moved his grocery bag to the seat between them.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: The development typically breaks the exposition's themes into short fragments and moves them quickly through several keys, which gives the section its restless sound.
story:
The community centre's music room smelled of old carpet and instant coffee, and Jesse had claimed the corner table by the window because it was the only one with a working outlet for the laptop. He was there for the third Thursday in a row, headphones on, a photocopied score of Mozart's Sonata in A major flattened under his palms, trying to hear what Ms. Schneider kept telling him he wasn't hearing yet. The theory exam was in eleven days. If he passed it, the conservatory would let him into the second-year analysis class without repeating the foundations course he'd tested out of by a single mark.

Izaiah arrived twenty minutes late with a bag of chips and no apologies, the way he always did. He dropped into the chair across from Jesse and stole one headphone, holding it a few inches from his ear like it might bite. "This is the stormy one," he said. The development section was playing, the piano crashing through a minor key, and Jesse nodded without looking up.

"Here's the thing," Jesse said, pausing the recording. "I can mark the exposition fine. First theme, second theme, the repeat sign, all in the right bars. And the recapitulation is obvious because it's the opening tune again. But the middle just sounds like chaos to me. I can't tell where anything begins, so I can't prove where the development starts when I write it up." He slid the score across the table. "Ms. Schneider says that's where the marks are."

Izaiah chewed, unbothered, and reached over to restart the track from the middle. "Listen again, then. You played me the opening in the car last week, like forty times." He tilted the borrowed headphone toward Jesse's head. The storm rolled on, fragments of melody tossed between the hands, landing in one key and immediately being shoved into another. Jesse bent over the score with a pencil, following the sixteenth notes bar by bar, and then he stopped. Four notes in the bass, quick and buried, and he knew them. It was the opening tune, broken into a shard, wearing minor like a disguise.

"That's it," Jesse said. "That's the first theme, right there, but it's only four notes and then it's gone." He tapped the bar. "The whole development is doing this. It takes the exposition's themes and smashes them into these short fragments, and it moves them through keys so fast you can't get your footing. That's why it sounds restless. It's not new material at all, it's the old material taken apart." He wrote the words in the margin, and his hand was steady, and for the first time the section had edges he could trace.

Izaiah leaned back. "So what's the problem, then? Sounds like you cracked it."

"The problem is I have to say something about it, not just label it. And everything I come up with sounds either like Ms. Schneider talking or like nothing at all." Jesse pulled his notebook over. He had two pages of half-thoughts. One argued that the fragments made the music feel unstable on purpose, that the restlessness was the point. The other, older page, argued almost the opposite, that Mozart was just following procedure, sonata form as a container he poured the same craft into every time, and any feeling was the listener's projection. The two positions had been sitting in his notebook for a week refusing to speak to each other.

He looked at the bar with the four hidden notes. The second position would call that a mechanical reminiscence, required by convention. The first position would call it a memory surfacing in a storm. He thought about his father, who liked to say that anything written before 1900 was reactionary decoration for people afraid of the present, and about how wrong that had always sounded to Jesse without his being able to say why. Maybe the honest answer was that both things were true at once, and the score didn't force you to choose, and the choice was the analysis. He wrote one line across the divide between the two pages: the fragments are procedure made audible as feeling, and what remains uncertain is whether Mozart heard it that way too.

When Ms. Schneider came by on her way out, Jesse turned the notebook so she could see the margin notes and the pencilled brackets around the development. She read for a long moment, longer than she usually gave anything, and then set the score down in front of him with the page open to the beginning.

"Play me the exposition," she said. "Then the development. From the top, and this time you decide where the second one starts." Jesse pulled the headphones off, set his hands above the photocopied keys of the score as if it were a piano, and gave the downbeat with his pencil.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back in student housing found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.
story:
The moving truck was due at the new house by four o'clock, which meant Violet had until noon to say goodbye to everyone she had ever loved, and she was spending that time wedged in the back of her mother's station wagon between Marion and Ryker while her father circled the same block for the third time because he refused to stop and ask for directions to the highway.

"Stop at the diner," Marion said. "Ten minutes. I'll buy you the goodbye pancakes."

"We don't have ten minutes. We have a truck in Connecticut by four."

"You have your whole life in Connecticut," Ryker said, which was meant to be funny and landed somewhere else entirely, so he looked out the window at the gas station they were not stopping at.

Marion had brought a shoebox of things she was calling "evidence," which she kept lifting the lid of to peek at, and Violet had spent the last six miles trying not to ask what was inside, because asking felt like agreeing that something was ending. Her father took the ramp onto the interstate with the dour concentration of a man who believed the truck was a moral test he intended to pass.

"Okay," Marion said finally, opening the box on her knees. "Item one." It was a folded napkin from the eighth-grade dance, the one where Marion had cried and Violet had told everyone it was allergies, and Ryker had gone along with it, and the three of them had never spoken of the arrangement aloud, though they all understood they were bound by it, a complicity so old it had stopped feeling like a choice.

"You kept that?"

"I kept everything. Item two is the schedule from chemistry, which is less romantic but I feel is important documentation."

Violet laughed, and then, because she was tired of the box making everything feel like a funeral, she said, "Can I tell you the thing I found out? The thing I've been obsessing about for a week?"

Ryker said, "Is it about the truck?"

"It is never about the truck. There was this study, 1950, these researchers, Festinger, Schachter, and Back. Student housing. They found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends."

"Meaning what, exactly?" Marion said.

"Meaning you three months from now are statistically doomed to love whoever has the locker next to yours. Meaning it's not fate, it's architecture."

Her father said from the front, "Who's paying for that education," but not unkindly.

Violet had found the study at two in the morning, spiraling, and it had worked on her like a hot iron on a wound, cauterizing the panic for a moment, sealing it off. Because if friendship was partly just proximity, then what she had with Marion and Ryker was not less real, exactly, but it was less chosen than she had believed, and she had been turning that over ever since. She had never lived within four blocks of either of them. They had been assigned the same lab table in ninth grade, the same bus route since kindergarten, the same stairwell for three years, and every one of those things had been done to her rather than by her. She said some of this out loud, carefully, watching their faces.

"So we're an accident of zoning," Marion said. "Wonderful. I love being a municipality's love child."

"That's not what I mean. Or it is what I mean, but I don't know what to do with it. If closeness makes friends, then distance should unmake them, except there was that girl in our grade who moved to Ohio and came back a year later with her Ohio best friend, so distance made her a friend too. Proximity and absence both work. It can't be both simple and true." She heard herself and stopped. "I don't actually have a conclusion. I've been trying to get one for a week and I don't have it."

Ryker was quiet for a while, long enough that the odometer ticked over another mile. "The stairwell," he said. "The one from the study. It's a thing that's true about everybody, not about you specifically. Nobody's ever going to do a study about whether Violet comes back."

"I could be a study," Violet said. "Sample size of one. Deeply flawed methodology."

"Peer review by Marion," he said.

"I'd reject you," Marion said, "but gently, with useful comments."

Her father took the exit he had refused to take directions for, which turned out to be the correct exit, and pulled into the diner lot, and put the car in park with a decisive clunk. "Ten minutes," he said. "Not one more. The truck does not wait."

The three of them went in and the waitress poured coffee nobody had ordered and Marion opened the shoebox at the table, item by item, and when she got to the bottom there was a blank index card and a pen, and she slid both across to Violet without a word.

"For what?"

"Documentation," Marion said. "First entry. Write down who sits near you."

Violet picked up the pen and wrote, at the top of the card, Stairwell, and underlined it twice.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, a ball dropped from a table and a ball launched horizontally from the same height hit a level floor at the same time.
story:
Isabelle had built the ramp herself, from balsa wood and a hinge she had borrowed from her father's toolbox and never returned, and she was certain it would work, because she was generally certain of things, and because the physics, she felt, was on her side. The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and vinegar from the cleaning solution someone had spilled near the bake sale table. Behind her, Shannon was arranging the two steel ball bearings on the table like a magician laying out cards.

"You're going to lose this bet," Isabelle said. "The one that rolls off the edge travels farther. It has to stay in the air longer. That's just sense."

Samantha, who had brought her own stopwatch and a notebook with a page ruled into two columns, looked up. "I don't think sense has anything to do with it. Sense says heavy things fall faster, and sense is wrong about that too."

"Fine. Then we test it." Isabelle had agreed to the bet on Tuesday, mostly to have something to hang the project on, and partly because Shannon had suggested they monetize the whole fair, charge a dollar per demonstration, and Isabelle had said no so quickly that she now suspected she was the one who was nervous. She adjusted the ramp so its end was level with the tabletop, and set the drop chute beside it, so that one ball would simply fall straight down from the same height while the other left the edge moving horizontally. A meter stick below marked where each one landed. She had rehearsed the explanation a dozen times in the mirror, her voice steady, cerebral, calm, and she was still surprised every time the mirror showed her hands.

The gym filled slowly. Ms. Chowdhury came by at ten with her clipboard and her reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and stood at the edge of the booth with the particular stillness of a teacher deciding whether to intervene. "Run it," she said, which was not a question.

Isabelle released both balls at once. She was watching the rolling one, the launched one, the one she was sure would take its time, would hang, would arrive late like a guest who had farther to travel. She heard one sound. She waited for the second.

One sound. A single click on the floor, both bearings striking together, so close in time that the gym's echo turned them into one.

"That can't be right," Isabelle said. She picked up the balls. Her hands, she noticed with some irritation, were doing exactly what the mirror had warned her about. She ran it again, and again, Samantha leaning in with the stopwatch, Shannon crouched at floor level with her ear an inch from the tile. Dropped and launched, from the same height, one ball falling straight and the other flying out sideways, and every single time the two clicks came down as one.

"The horizontal doesn't slow the fall," Samantha said quietly, writing in her column. "It just moves it over."

Isabelle stood very still. All week she had been splitting velocities in her practice problems, separating the sideways part from the up-and-down part, treating them like two separate debts owed to two separate creditors, and she had done it correctly on paper, and she had still not believed it. She had believed her own certainty instead, which was, she was beginning to see, a different and less reliable instrument. She thought about how she would tell her father about the lost bet, how she would describe standing in a gymnasium hearing one sound where she had promised herself there would be two.

"Okay," she said. "I owe you both a milkshake. And I owe the ramp an apology."

"Take the apology back," Shannon said. "It did exactly what you built it to do."

By eleven the demonstration had a small crowd, two freshmen and a boy from the robotics club who kept asking about friction, and Isabelle had found her rhythm. She stopped performing the speech she had rehearsed and started doing the thing itself, releasing the balls, letting people crouch and listen, watching their faces at the single click the way Samantha must have watched hers. When a freshman asked how it could possibly work, she said, "I could tell you, or you could put your ear down there," and the freshman knelt on the waxed floor in his good jacket.

Ms. Chowdhury came back at noon, without the clipboard this time. She watched three runs in silence, arms folded. "So which one lands first?" she asked the crowd, and Isabelle opened her mouth to answer, then closed it, then gestured at the floor.

"Lie down and find out," she said.

Ms. Chowdhury, to Isabelle's lasting astonishment, got down on one knee, tilted her head, and waited for the sound.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Spike tape is coloured tape used to mark where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor.
story:
The black box theatre smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Ryan had three weeks to make something of it. Mr. Farah-Ali had handed him the one-act with the flat encouragement of a man distributing cafeteria trays: here is your portion, good luck, do not complain about the menu. Ryan had wanted to direct since he was fourteen, when he'd watched a student production fall apart in real time and felt, obscurely, that he could have saved it. Now the script was his and the actors were his and the sinking suspicion was also his, arriving nightly around seven o'clock.

His actors were Martha, who could act, and Kiptyn, who could not but who had auditioned with a confidence Ryan envied and could not direct. Martha played the daughter returning home; Kiptyn played the sofa's owner, a silent father who sat and read a newspaper through two of the play's three scenes. The blocking had seemed simple on paper. In practice, whenever Ryan looked away, the sofa migrated. Kiptyn hauled it toward centre stage for comfort, or the stage crew shoved it against the back wall to clear the entrance, and every night Ryan arrived to find the geography of the family altered without consultation.

"Your dad can't be twelve feet away when you tell him about the letter," Ryan said on the fourth rehearsal. He stood in the audience seats, arms crossed, aware that he was mimicking every director he had ever disliked.

"He's distant," Kiptyn said. "It's a choice."

"It's a choice you're making with furniture."

Martha, resting her chin on the sofa arm, watched them like someone at a tennis match she'd already seen. She was the only one of them taking it seriously without taking it personally, and Ryan was beginning to understand that this was the whole job. He had spent the first rehearsals being either a tyrant or an apologist for the script, apologizing to the actors for every line that felt unnatural, apologizing to the playwright for the actors, apologizing generally to the art form. Neither mode worked. Kiptyn walked all over the apologist and dug in against the tyrant, and the sofa continued its slow continental drift.

The fifth rehearsal, Ryan arrived early and found Mr. Farah-Ali kneeling at the edge of the stage with a cardboard box, pulling out rolls of tape in yellow and blue and a violent pink. He set them on the apron without ceremony and left, which was the most useful thing he had done all week. Ryan turned a roll over in his hands and thought about dance studios, about the bright L-shapes taped to gym floors that marked where the routine began.

He tore a length of the pink and pressed an L against the stage floor at each corner of the sofa. Then he marked Martha's starting position in blue, two crosses near the door, and Kiptyn's chair in yellow, angled so the newspaper caught the light. When the actors came in, Kiptyn looked at the floor and then at Ryan with something like betrayal.

"What is that," he said.

"Spike tape," Ryan said. "It marks where things go." He let the silence do the rest, and after a moment Kiptyn dragged the sofa back onto its pink corners, grumbling, and sat, and opened his newspaper. It was, Ryan noted, exactly where the sofa belonged. What he hadn't expected was Martha: she stood on her blue crosses, tested them, and then asked whether they could mark her path through the second scene, because she'd been inventing it fresh each night and wanted it to stop being an improvisation and start being hers. He hadn't planned to block her movement at all. He'd thought of the tape as discipline, as a fence against chaos, and she was asking to use it as a memory.

They ran the scene. The sofa stayed. Martha crossed to the window on her marks and paused there, and Kiptyn lowered his newspaper a half inch, which was more response than he'd given in five rehearsals, and Ryan sat in the third row with the tape roll going soft and warm in his hand. He still didn't know whether the production would be any good, whether firmness and openness were both possible in the same voice, whether he was directing a play or just decorating a floor with a grid. But when Martha asked if they could go again, he stood up and said, "From the top. Sofa's on its marks." Kiptyn sighed the sigh of a conquered nation, and snapped his newspaper open.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
story:
The licensing office smelled of vending machine coffee and wet umbrellas, and Levi had been standing in line for forty minutes with a folder of paperwork his mother had assembled with the seriousness of a legal brief. Behind him, Dana kept reading the permit study guide over his shoulder, occasionally humming a wrong answer just to watch his jaw tighten. When the clerk finally called him forward, she took the folder, stamped two of the pages, and slid a laminated card across the counter like a dealer laying down a card she already knew he wouldn't like.

"Congratulations," she said. "Learner's permit."

Layton arrived at the parking lot ten minutes later, leaning out his passenger window with the windows still up, which meant his voice arrived slightly before he did. "So Saturday," he called through the glass. "You drive, we ride, we get milkshakes, I don't have to beg my sister for the car. This is the beginning of an era."

Levi turned the permit over in his hands. On the back, in type so small it seemed almost embarrassed, was a paragraph about restrictions. He read it twice, and something in his chest went quiet in a way he recognized from the moment a teacher says "before we begin, everyone pass your essays forward."

"Actually," he said, "hang on."

Ms. Sokolov, the instructor who would take him out for his first lesson that afternoon, was waiting by a white sedan with a magnetic sign on the door. She was retired from something she never specified and had the calm of a person who had seen four decades of teenagers aim cars at mailboxes. She watched Levi read the back of the card and did not interrupt, which he appreciated, because Dana and Layton were already expatiating on the milkshake itinerary, the route, the playlist, the specific toppings.

"Here's the thing," Levi said, holding up the card. "This is a learner's permit. It's the first stage. There's a whole system, graduated licensing, where you go from the permit to a provisional license before the real one. And the provisional one has restrictions too. So basically, for a long time, no friends in the car."

Layton lowered his window at last, as if the glass had been protecting him from the news. "You're telling me the government has an opinion about whether I can hold a milkshake in your passenger seat."

"The government has many opinions," Ms. Sokolov said mildly, gathering clipboards from the trunk. "Most of them involve paperwork."

Here was the part Levi had been turning over all morning, ever since his mother had mentioned the rules at breakfast and he had pretended he already knew. He had walked into the licensing office imagining freedom, the whole smooth highway of it, and walked out holding a card that was, essentially, a training wheel. His first instinct had been to feel cheated. His second instinct, slower and more honest, was that he had seen how Layton drove, and how Dana commented on how Layton drove, and that maybe a year of driving alone with an adult in the passenger seat was less a punishment than an armistice between him and the two tons of metal he was about to be responsible for. He couldn't decide which instinct was the real one. He suspected they could both be true at once, which was annoying.

"So Saturday is off," Layton said, with the gravity of a man canceling a summit.

"Saturday is off for months," Levi said. "Possibly most of the year."

"Most of the year," Dana repeated, to no one, to the parking lot, to the universe, which had clearly wronged him personally.

"Get in the car anyway," Ms. Sokolov said, and Layton, confused by his own feet, got in the back seat of the driving school sedan while Dana took the passenger side, so that Levi's first lesson began with an audience, which was exactly what the permit was designed to prevent. She made them both get out. She made them stand behind a concrete pillar. "You can watch," she said. "Watching is legal."

The first twenty minutes were humbling. He stalled twice, though the car was automatic, which Layton declared, from behind the pillar, a congenital talent, something he was born with, an inborn gift for stopping vehicles without touching them. Ms. Sokolov said nothing, which was somehow worse and also better. By the third lap of the parking lot his hands had stopped inventing their own steering technique, and when she told him to pull out onto the side street, he did it without killing anyone, including the pigeon that had been standing in the road with what he felt was excessive confidence.

Afterward, everyone ended up at the milkshake place anyway, Dana driving, Layton riding shotgun with the toppings list, Levi in the back with his permit and a large chocolate malt. It was not the era they had planned. It was, provisionally, the era they had, and Levi found he could live with a provisional era, provided there was chocolate in it.

Layton raised his shake. "To the provisional era."

"To the restrictions," Dana said.

"To the pigeon," Levi said, and they touched the cups together over the center console, gently, the way you do when nothing is fully settled yet.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote: 35 senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed.
story:
Grandfather's study smelled of pipe tobacco he hadn't smoked in six years, and Laurence spread her notes across the desk where his old ledgers used to sit. The house was hers for the afternoon. Her mother had dropped her off with a casserole and the instruction to "keep him company," which everyone in the family understood to mean check that he was still eating properly, and which Laurence had quietly translated into three uninterrupted hours with her politics outline before the exam on Friday.

She was supposed to compare how the two systems choose and remove a head of government, and she had decided, in the confident way she decided things, that the parliamentary side was obviously better. A prime minister who loses the confidence of parliament can be gone by Thursday. A president clings on for a full term no matter how despised. It seemed so clean, so obviously fair, that she'd nearly stopped thinking about it, which was exactly what Mr. Chatterjee had warned her about in September, in that mild voice he used when he was being merciless. "You argue like someone who has never lost anything," he'd said, and she'd laughed, and then hadn't.

The floorboards creaked in the hall, and her grandfather appeared in the doorway with two mugs, though she'd asked for nothing. "Your mother said you'd be working," he said. "Working is better with tea." He set the spare mug beside her elbow, then lowered himself into the chair by the window and stayed there, watching the garden, or possibly watching her. He did that more since grandmother died. He wanted her in the room, she understood that much, though he would never say it, and so she let him stay even though she worked worse with an audience.

Her phone buzzed. Karly, from the study group: "did you find the johnson thing." Laurence had promised to look it up, and had half-looked it up, and now she typed it properly while her grandfather's eyes moved over the same screen from his chair, no shame in him about reading other people's messages. In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote. Thirty-five senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed. She read it twice. One vote. A president had come within a single senator of removal, and the bar had held.

"One vote," her grandfather said. "You look like that over one vote."

"A whole president," she said. "Almost removed. One person said no, or enough people did, and he stayed."

He was quiet for a moment, and she thought he'd gone back to the garden. Then he said, "And is that a good thing or a bad thing?"

She started to say bad, obviously, because a president who nearly got removed and didn't had escaped something, hadn't he. But her own argument caught her. If removal were easy, she'd written that morning, a parliamentary-style no-confidence vote would let a bare majority eviscerate a leader mid-term, overturn an election on a whim. The two-thirds bar was the armistice between the two sides of government, the truce that said: you may despise him, but you must despise him overwhelmingly before you touch him. She hadn't meant to argue for the other side. The notes had done it without asking her.

"That's the trouble with you," her grandfather said, though he said it fondly, she was fairly sure it was fondly. "You find a thing and suddenly the thing you knew isn't the thing anymore."

"It's not that I didn't know it," she said, which was, she'd admit later only to herself, not entirely true. She had known the number. She had written thirty-five in the margin of her notes on Tuesday and had kept writing past it, because it was inconvenient, because it made her neat essay into two essays. She'd told Karly she couldn't find it. She typed now, slowly: found it. it's real. 35 to convict, one short of two-thirds, acquitted by one vote. Karly replied with three exclamation points and then, a minute later, "so which side are we taking friday," and Laurence sat with her thumbs over the screen, wanting to say the easy side, the side she'd already drafted.

Mr. Chatterjee had asked them, at the last session, whether they could hold a position and still see past it, and she had said yes too quickly. Here in the spartan little study, at the desk with the pipe smell and the borrowed mug going cold, she thought she finally could, and also that she still wasn't sure what she believed, and that both of those things might be true at once, and that Friday was coming either way.

Her grandfather leaned forward in his chair. "So tell me," he said. "The one who voted no. What do you suppose he was thinking?"

She looked up at him, and then down at the number she'd been ignoring all week. "I don't know," she said. "But I'm going to find out before Friday."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The US Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 and reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July 2023.
story:
Maya knew how interest rates worked. She had known since Tuesday, which was when she'd written the flashcards, and knowing for four days was practically the same as knowing for a semester. The quiz was tomorrow morning, third period, and tonight the four of them had claimed the corner table by the library windows, where the late sun came in sideways and warmed the spines of the economics textbooks nobody ever opened for pleasure.

"Ask me," she said, tapping the deck.

Daxton took the cards without being asked. He'd been scanning the practice questions all afternoon with the particular hunger of someone who needed an A the way other people needed air, and he riffled the stack now as though the cards themselves owed him something. "All right. Why does a central bank raise its policy rate when inflation is high?"

"Because expensive money slows everything down." She said it quickly, the way you say a thing you've said before. "Higher rates make borrowing costlier, so people take out fewer loans, so they spend less, and when spending cools, prices stop climbing so fast. Demand eases. That's the whole machine."

"Beautiful," Daxton said, and flipped the card over, and Maya didn't look at the back because she didn't need to.

Gabriel had been quiet, dismantling a granola bar into its component oats, which was his habit when he was deciding whether to say something. He was the one who'd actually read the chapter, twice, and the one whose questions in class Ms. Ramos always answered slowly, as if choosing her words from a limited supply. "When," he said finally. "Rates started going up from basically nothing. When was that?"

Maya opened her mouth. Nothing came out that had a date attached to it. The window glass held a smudge where someone had pressed a forehead against it, probably weeks ago, and she looked at the smudge for a second longer than the smudge deserved. "Recently," she said.

"It's not a trick question." Gabriel was not gloating, which somehow made it worse. He never gloated, which Maya had once pathologized to Daxton as a form of showing off, a reverse vanity, though she'd admitted by now that this said more about her than about Gabriel. "It's on the sheet Ms. Ramos gave us. The Fed began raising the policy rate from near zero in March 2022, and by July 2023 it was between 5.25 and 5.50 percent. That's the part everyone forgets, the numbers."

"That's one part," Daxton said. "There are forty other parts. Skip it." He moved to the next card, but the next card was about supply shocks, and Maya found she was still sitting with the date, March 2022, feeling the strange vertigo of learning that something she'd been confidently narrating had happened in the background of her own life, unmarked. She'd been fifteen. She'd been worried about a swim meet that spring.

Here is what she would not say out loud, that evening or later: she had believed she understood the mechanism the way you believe you know a route you've driven only as a passenger. The night before, her mother had called from the bank parking lot, reading numbers off two mortgage offers, her voice tight with the flatness Maya recognized as worry worn smooth. "Why is everything so different from three years ago," her mother had asked, not really asking, and Maya had said, "The Fed changed things," and had felt, saying it, the small fraudulent glow of a person using a word she couldn't unpack. She had hung up and made the flashcards. The flashcards were, she could admit at this table if pressed, an ancillary comfort, a way of appearing to study the hole she'd papered over with her mother on the phone.

So she took the cards back from Daxton, who protested that they had a system, and there were only three hours left before the library closed and the quiz opened, and the deadline was real in the way only school deadlines are real, harmless and absolute at once. "Gabriel," she said. "Ask me the whole thing. Dates included."

He did. She said it back to him, the Fed raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022, reaching a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July 2023, and then, because a date without a reason was just a number, she kept going, walking the chain out loud: costlier loans, less borrowing, cooler spending, easing pressure on prices. Somewhere in the middle of saying it, the route stopped being a passenger's route. She could feel where the turns were, and also where the map ran out, because Gabriel raised his hand mildly and said, "And how long does that take? Who gets hurt on the way?" and Maya said, honestly, "I don't know yet. That part's not on the cards."

Ms. Ramos passed the table on her rounds, pausing at the stack. "You've got chicanery written on this one," she said, tapping a card where Maya had scrawled the word after finding it in a column about misleading loan terms. "Wrong unit. But I like the ambition."

Daxton claimed the cards back and drilled them at double speed, hunting his A, while Gabriel swept his oat dust into his palm and the sun moved off the window entirely, leaving the smudge in shadow. Maya texted her mother before the library closed: the numbers from the two offers, plus one question, which bank officer said which.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: One of Amazon's leadership principles, 'Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit', asks employees to respectfully challenge a decision they disagree with, then commit fully once it is made.
story:
The back room of Riverbend Stone & Garden smelled of wet gravel and the lemon cleaner Ms. Morales used on the display counters, and Kayla had learned in her first week that the smell meant Saturday had officially begun. She stacked the last flat of river rocks beside the loading door and went looking for Hajar, who was supposed to be pricing the new shipment of flagstone but was instead standing very still in aisle four, holding a printed email like it might bite her.

"They changed the plan," Hajar said. "For the front courtyard. Remember how we pitched the sedimentary display, the layered limestone wall showing the cross-section, education corner, little cards about how each layer formed? Ms. Morales approved it Tuesday. Now corporate wants the front filled with the pre-cut paver kits instead, and the education corner gets moved to the side lot by the fence."

Kayla took the email from her. It was written in the flat, tidy style her father called corporate speak, each sentence structured like a small fenced yard: objective, rationale, timeline. "Enhance visibility of high-margin product at primary entrance," it said, and "Reposition educational display to secondary location by end of week." She read it twice, partly because she genuinely wanted to catch every clause, and partly because stalling gave her time to decide whether to be angry in front of Hajar or alone later, in the walk-in cooler where the sod was kept.

Archer came around the corner with a dolly and a donut in the same hand, which was against at least two rules. "I already heard," he said through the donut. "Dominga from the front desk told me. What are you going to do, write them a strongly worded memo?" He grinned, but Hajar didn't, and Kayla noticed that Hajar's face had gone into the particular stillness she used whenever an adult had disappointed her, the same face from junior year when the principal cut the arts assembly for a second time.

"It's not about a memo," Kayla said. "It's about how you disagree when the decision isn't yours. My cousin works at Amazon and she told me about it once. One of their leadership principles is called 'Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit.' You're supposed to respectfully challenge a decision you disagree with, and then, once it's made, commit to it completely." She heard herself say it and worried it sounded like a poster in a guidance counselor's office, but Hajar was actually listening, so she kept going. "The backbone part and the commit part. Both. Not one."

Archer licked sugar off his thumb. "So the company that does that is telling us to move the wall."

"The principle isn't theirs, they just wrote it down," Kayla said. "And it's not the worst instruction I've ever heard." She thought of the time in middle school she'd sulked through an entire group project because her poster idea lost the vote, how she'd let the whole presentation droop to prove a point nobody at the table could even remember now. She did not say any of this out loud. Some admissions you make only to the gravel.

They found Ms. Morales in the front courtyard, on her knees, already pulling the first course of limestone from the education wall. Her phone lay in the mulch beside her, the email open, and she had the look of someone doing a thing carefully so that no one could ascribe to her any carelessness in the doing. "I know," she said before Kayla spoke. "I argued for keeping it. Two emails, one phone call. I said the school groups come for that wall, that the kids touch the fossils and ask how old they are, and I get to say 'older than anything in this parking lot by a margin of antiquity you can't picture.' I lost. So now the wall comes down by Friday, and I'm taking it down myself so it's done right."

"You're not even mad?" Hajar said.

"I'm plenty mad," Ms. Morales said, sitting back on her heels. "But I made my case to the people who could change the decision, I made it politely, I brought the signup sheets from the school visits, and they said no. If I do a sloppy teardown to show how I feel, the wall gets damaged and nobody learns anything except that I'm sulky. If I do it well, the pieces survive, and maybe in six months I bring back the visit numbers and propose the side lot turns out better than we think. Mad and committed aren't opposites. You can hold both."

Kayla crouched and lifted the second course of stone, the one with the brachiopod imprint that the fourth graders always fought over touching first. It was heavier than she expected, and cold, and the imprint fit her thumb exactly. "Then we do it properly," she said. "Cards, photos before it comes apart, we could even label the pieces so if it gets rebuilt someone knows the order."

Hajar pulled out her phone and started photographing the layers, top to bottom, methodical, the way she took notes in biology. "I'll write up the documentation tonight," she said. "Structured. Headings. They can't say we didn't care just because we disagreed."

Archer parked the dolly, wiped his hands on his jeans, and for once didn't make a joke. He knelt in the mulch and began separating the thin fossiliferous slabs from the thicker base stones, sorting them into two careful rows. "I still think it's a stupid decision," he said.

"Me too," Kayla said. "Hand me the next one."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together.
story:
The moving truck idled at the curb while Seth counted the boxes on the lawn, because counting was a thing he could do, unlike making the street feel like a place he lived. Thirty-one boxes, one bicycle with a flat tire, and a lawn he did not have to mow, which his father called a perk and Seth called another sign that nothing here belonged to him yet. The street was called Fallow Ridge, which sounded to Seth like a place that had given up on growing anything.

A girl appeared from the house next door, carrying a plate covered in foil, walking with the brisk confidence of someone delivering a diplomatic document. "I'm Blair," she said. "We made lemon bars, which is a lie, my mom made lemon bars, but I carried them, which is the part that matters." Seth took the plate. She looked at the boxes, then at him, appraising. "So you're the new draft pick. What position?"

"I don't really play anything."

"Everybody plays something here. Even Mr. Ferreira plays something, and he's roughly the age of the hills." She pointed her chin at the house across the street, where an older man was watering a garden with visible suspicion, as though the plants might try something. "He'll bring you tomatoes by Thursday. It's practically an ontology with him. You are a neighbor, therefore you receive tomatoes. That's the whole category of being."

Seth laughed for the first time in three days, the sound surprising him. That night he called Jillian, who was still back home, still at the lunch table he used to sit at, and the call lasted an hour and a half and covered nothing important and mattered more than anything else that had happened all week. She told him about the substitute who had mispronounced her name in four separate ways, and he told her about the tomato ontology, and they were both laughing when his mother knocked on the door to say it was midnight, two time zones ahead of Jillian, and that some of them had jobs in the morning.

The next day Blair found him sitting on his front steps with his phone open to a search. He had been doing math, the desperate kind, at eleven at night. "Okay," she said, dropping onto the step beside him without ceremony. "You have the face of a person doing sad arithmetic. What are we calculating?"

"How long it takes to make a friend," Seth said. "I found this study. Jeffrey Hall, 2018. He estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together. More than two hundred hours. Like, actually together."

Blair took the phone and read, her eyebrows going up in stages. "Two hundred hours. That's like, what, fifty school lunches? A whole summer of hanging out?" She handed it back. "Is this about the girl you called last night until your mom staged an intervention? Because I have ears, and also your window is ten feet from my porch."

"Jillian," Seth said. "We've been friends since fourth grade. I did the math on us too. I got to over two thousand hours before I stopped counting, and that's lowballing it. Bus rides alone, I figured three hundred." He looked at the phone. "So the math says I can't replace that here. And it also says the only way to start is to put in hours, which means hours here, which means I have to actually, I don't know, be here."

"That is the most loquacious way anyone has ever said 'hang out with me,'" Blair said. "But sure, I'll start your clock. Consider this hour one. Actually, consider the lemon bars hour zero, we're not wasting the lemon bars." She stood and brushed off her jeans. "Come on. We're going to meet Mr. Ferreira, because if you're going to log hours, the tomato man is free minutes, and also I need him to stop asking me whether the new kid plays anything."

They crossed the street, and Mr. Ferreira set down his hose with the expression of a man whose tomato ontology had just been confirmed by the universe. "You'll be the one in the yellow house," he said, as though verifying a prophecy. "You play anything? Music? Chess? I've been trying to find a chess opponent for six years."

"I mostly just talk," Seth said.

"Talking," said Mr. Ferreira, and smiled, and began inspecting him for tomato-worthiness. "Talking I can work with."

Blair leaned in behind the old man's shoulder and mouthed, "Hour two, don't screw it up." Seth nodded, stooped to examine the nearest tomato, and asked what kind it was.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, US workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of $899, compared with $708 for those without one.
story:
The hallway outside the gym smelled like floor wax and lilies, and Oliver kept the envelope flat against his thigh so no one would ask what was in it. Charlize had already asked twice. She was wearing her gown open over jeans, holding her cap by its elastic like a fish she'd caught, and Elie was pacing the trophy case as though the plaques might lean down and tell him something.

"You're doing the face," Charlize said. "The face you did before the regional final. The face you did before you asked Ms. Hussain for the extension."

"I'm not doing a face."

"You're doing the face," Elie said, from the trophy case, without turning around.

The truth, which Oliver had not told them, was that the envelope held a slip from the main office, and the slip said his participation in the ceremony was pending clearance of an obligation, and the obligation was listed only by a code number. He had until the line formed at six. It was 5:41. The crepuscular light through the hallway's high windows made everything look like a memory of itself, which he found unbearable, so he looked at the floor instead.

"I'll be right back," he said.

"Where," Charlize said, but he was already moving, past the juniors who'd come to watch, past a freshman selling candy bars for the robotics team, toward the history office where Ms. Hussain was pinning her hood with two hands and a mouthful of straight pins. She saw him and took the pins out of her mouth.

"Mr. Ahmadi," she said. "Walking tonight?"

"That's the question, actually." He handed her the slip. She read it, and her eyebrows did something small and private, and she went to her filing cabinet, which was old enough that the drawer shrieked. She came back with a paperback copy of a book Oliver had never seen in his life. "Gatsby," she said, "checked out under your name in September of your junior year. Sixty-one dollars to replace."

"That's not mine. I returned mine. I returned it late, but I returned it, I remember the night, it was raining."

"Then someone shelved it wrong and this copy wandered into my room instead of the library." She weighed it in her hand. "The system doesn't care whose hands it passed through. The system delimits: your name, your debt, your walk." She set it on the desk between them, and for a moment they both looked at it, the green cover, the price sticker from a used bookstore twelve miles away, some other edition entirely.

He thought about his uncle at dinner last month, the one who'd leaned back with his glass and said that a diploma was worth exactly this much and no more: for workers twenty-five and up, the ones with the diploma had median weekly earnings of eight hundred ninety-nine dollars, and the ones without had seven hundred and eight. Eighteen more a day, give or take. His uncle had said it like a verdict, like the whole thing had been weighed and found to be a modest thing. Oliver had spent weeks treating that number as an acquittal of his own doubt, proof that the paper mattered, that the walking mattered, that the four years had purchased something you could hold.

Standing in the office with a book he had never touched, he began to think his uncle had drawn the boundary in the wrong place. The slip on the desk said he owed sixty-one dollars for a book that was not his, and the ceremony would go on without him if he didn't pay it, and neither of those facts had anything to do with eight hundred ninety-nine dollars a week. The money attached to the diploma. The ceremony attached to something else, something to do with Charlize's fish-holding grip on her cap and Elie pacing the trophies like a man waiting on trial results.

"Can I pay it Monday?" he asked.

"The system says no."

"Then here's what I have." He turned out his pockets onto her desk: a ten, some ones, a movie stub, sixty-two cents in coins that rolled and settled. "Twenty-three dollars and the movie stub."

Ms. Hussain looked at the pile. Then she looked at him, and he could see her deciding something, the same way she decided extensions, the way she once let a whole class retake a test because one student's grandmother had died and she refused to delimit mercy to a single person. She opened her drawer again, the shriek, and came out with a checkbook.

"Thirty-eight dollars," she said, writing. "You'll owe me, and I will collect, and not in dollars. I'll want an email at Christmas telling me one true thing about your first semester."

"That's the interest?"

"That's the interest."

He carried the green book back down the hallway with the signed slip folded inside it, and when Charlize saw his face she said, "You're doing a different face now, what happened," and Elie abandoned the trophy case to intercept him.

"Fine," Oliver said. "I'll tell you in line."

The line was already forming outside the gym, gowns rippling in the doorway's light, and somewhere behind them a tuba player warmed up a note that broke and started over. Elie straightened his cap. Charlize snapped hers on backwards, then thought better of it.

"So what's the book?" she asked.

"Long story," Oliver said. "It's mine now."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: David Ricardo set out comparative advantage in his 1817 book On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, using England and Portugal trading cloth and wine.
story:
Jesse was supposed to be restocking the canned tomatoes, but he had the economics review sheet propped against a case of olive oil, and he had read the same paragraph four times. The store was slow for a Sunday. Somewhere near the registers a floor buffer droned, and the produce mister had desiccated the spinach at the end of its cycle, the leaves going dry and gray along the top of the pile. His exam was Monday morning, first period, and question twelve on the review sheet read, in Ms. Hoang's tidy handwriting, "Explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading."

Lola came through the swinging doors from the stockroom with a cart of cereal boxes. She was studying for the same exam, but she had gone home the night before and watched a documentary about something else entirely, so she felt no obligation to be grim about it.

"Quiz me," Jesse said.

"Define comparative advantage."

"You take two countries," he began, and then stopped, because he could not remember which countries. He had known on Tuesday. On Tuesday he had written it on his hand before gym. "France and something. France and Spain, maybe. Wine and... cheese?"

"You're making that up."

"I'm not making it up, I'm remembering it badly. Those are different things."

"You should ask her."

"She's not here, Lola, she's at home. Teachers live at home on Sundays. That's the whole deal."

Ms. Hoang was, in fact, at the end of aisle four, comparing the unit prices of two bags of rice with the focus of a woman doing arithmetic she did not trust the shelf label to have done correctly. Jesse did not see her until Lola steered the cereal cart around the corner and nearly clipped her basket.

"Sorry, Ms. Hoang," Lola said. Then, with the pugnacious cheer of someone who has found an advantage and intends to press it: "Actually, perfect timing. Jesse has a question about the trade unit."

Ms. Hoang looked at Jesse. She did not offer to explain anything. She said, "What have you got so far?"

"France and Spain," Jesse said. "Wine and cheese."

"Wrong on all counts," she said, and put the smaller bag of rice in her basket. "But you already knew that, which is why you're standing here looking like the tomatoes fell on you. Go find it. You have a phone, I assume, or a textbook somewhere less damp than this aisle." She pushed her basket toward the registers and did not look back.

Jesse dried his hands on his apron and dug his phone out of his locker by the break room. The store's wifi reached only as far as the deli case, so he stood between the olive bar and a display of breath mints, scrolling, while Douglas sliced roast beef behind the counter and pretended not to be interested. Jesse found it in three places, and the third place said it plainly enough that he said it out loud.

"David Ricardo set out comparative advantage in his 1817 book On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, using England and Portugal trading cloth and wine."

"That's a sentence?" Douglas said.

"That's the sentence. England and Portugal, cloth and wine. Not France, not cheese."

"So which one's better at making stuff?"

"That's the part that's actually weird." Jesse turned his phone off and looked at the olive bar as though it might back him up. "Everyone assumes the point is that one country is better at everything and one is better at something else. But the example is England and Portugal, and the whole idea is that even if one of them is worse at both things, both still gain by trading. Ricardo made it up in 1817 and everyone's still arguing about it." He paused. "I can say the fact. I'm not sure I can say why it's true, not in a way that would hold up if Ms. Hoang asked a follow-up."

"That's most of what I know about anything," Douglas said, and went back to the roast beef.

Lola reappeared with the empty cereal cart. "Did you find it?"

"England and Portugal, cloth and wine, Ricardo, 1817." He said it twice more under his breath, the way he used to memorize locker combinations. "I still don't know if I can explain the both-gain part. That's the question that's actually worth thirty points."

"Then say what you do know and stop where it stops being true," Lola said. She took the review sheet off the olive oil case and handed it back to him. "That's what you told me to do on the French oral, and it worked."

At ten o'clock the floor buffer finally went quiet, and the manager sent Jesse to face the shelves in aisle six. He lined up the cans of tomatoes with their labels forward, and between rows he mouthed the sentence again. England and Portugal, cloth and wine, 1817. Somewhere in the middle of the aisle he stopped mouthing it and started trying it a different way, out loud, as if he were telling Douglas, and it came out steadier than before. He got to the end of the shelf, picked up the last can, and set it in place with the label facing out.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Economists count the wages a student gives up while studying full-time as part of the cost of college, along with tuition.
story:
The used Corolla sat in the third row of the lot, silver, dented above the rear wheel, priced at four thousand two hundred dollars, and Eli had circled it twice already when Ms. Singh came out of the glass office and found him there. She ran the paperwork side of the dealership and had known him since March, when he'd started washing cars on Saturdays, and she did not treat him the way she treated the customers, which was to say she did not pretend. "You've got three thousand six hundred saved," she said. "I've seen your envelope. You count it every break."

"It's four thousand one hundred now," Eli said. "Two more Saturdays."

She walked a slow ring around the Corolla the way she did around every car, one hand behind her back, and a voluble man in a linen jacket came off the lot toward them, talking before he'd arrived, a retired magistrate who apparently wanted a convertible and had opinions on every model in the inventory. Ms. Singh detached from Eli to handle him, and Eli stood by the Corolla and put his hand flat on the hood, still warm from the afternoon.

Four thousand one hundred dollars. He had earned it at nine dollars an hour, and he knew exactly how many Saturdays that was, because he had counted the Saturdays the way other people counted money. What he had not counted, until the open house in April, was everything the money was not. He had gone with Jasmin, who wanted the engineering program and had made a spreadsheet about it. At the financial aid table, while a counselor handed them brochures, Jasmin had looked at the tuition figure and said, "That's not even the real number." She said that economists count the wages a student gives up while studying full-time as part of the cost of college, along with tuition. She called that the opportunity cost, and then she'd added her own line, that four years of full-time work she'd never do was sitting inside that spreadsheet like a ghost in a cell. Eli had laughed, and then he hadn't.

He had been thinking about it wrong since, or at least incompletely. The car was not four thousand two hundred dollars. The car was four thousand two hundred dollars plus whatever the four thousand one hundred could have become, or prevented, or covered in October when the tuition bill came and the difference between attending and not attending got decided in a cashier's office by whoever was standing there with the money. The magistrate's voice carried across the lot, something about depreciation, something about how a car loses a third of its value the moment it leaves the lot, and Eli thought, well, at least the ghost depreciates too.

But there was the other accounting, the one his body kept. He was eighteen and had never driven to the ocean. He had turned down the summer trip with Sara because the trip cost eight hundred dollars and eight hundred was two and a half Saturdays of the car, except that now the car was also the college fund, so the trip had been turned down twice, once per ledger. He remembered standing in her driveway telling her no, and the way she'd nodded like it was fine, and how the drive home on his bicycle had taken forty minutes into a headwind. The car would exhilarate him; he was honest enough with himself to use that word, the exact physical lift of it, windows down, the whole county opening like a door. That was real. It was not less real for being hard to put in a spreadsheet.

Ms. Singh came back with the magistrate's paperwork, clipped and smiling, and set it on the desk by the window where Eli could see it through the glass. She caught him looking and came out again, keys in her hand. "The Corolla," she said. "You want to sit in it?"

"It's a big decision," Eli said.

"It's a Saturday job's worth of decision," she said. "It's also a decision about the fall." She didn't say which fall, or what she meant, and he understood that she had done the same arithmetic herself, years ago, in some form, and had landed somewhere, and that where she'd landed had a dealership around it, which could mean anything.

He got into the driver's seat. The upholstery smelled like someone else's life, pine air freshener and cold coffee. Through the windshield he could see the lot lights coming on, one row at a time, and past them the road out of town, empty in both directions. On the passenger seat Ms. Singh laid the keys, then took them back, then laid them down again.

"Two more Saturdays," she said. "You don't have to tell me today."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: A launch velocity v at an angle θ above the horizontal splits into a horizontal component v cos θ and a vertical component v sin θ.
story:
The textbook lay open on the kitchen table, its margins already crowded with Paige's pencil marks, and beside it her half of a shared physics problem set, due Monday. Her mother had gone to bed an hour ago, and the house had that particular late-August quiet where every small sound, the fridge hum, a car passing, seemed to collate itself into a single argument for giving up and going to sleep. Paige stayed. She had chosen to take physics instead of a second year of art, and the choosing had felt noble in June and felt expensive now, like most things she had decided on her own.

Her phone buzzed. Sunny, texting from three streets away, had made it a personal mission to pass physics before the soccer season started, because the coach had said something about eligibility and because, as Sunny put it, she refused to let a subject named after her lose her a season. "still on number 6?" the message read. "come over, im awake, also im impecunious again and your house has real snacks."

Paige sent back a thumbs up and texted Camila too, who showed up ten minutes later carrying an immunology textbook she had no reason to open until September but carried everywhere anyway, the way other people carried lucky coins. The three of them arranged themselves around the table, Sunny stealing a bag of pretzels from the pantry with the confidence of a regular, Camila sitting with her chin in her hand.

Number six was the problem. A ball launched at twelve meters per second at an angle of eight degrees above the horizontal, and the question was how far it traveled. Sunny went first, writing fast, the way she did everything, and announced that the ball would go nearly straight up and come down almost on the thrower's head. "Twelve times the sine of eight degrees," she said, tapping her calculator, "that's the vertical part, so basically all twelve meters per second is vertical. Look how small the angle is, it's almost nothing."

"That's the whole thing backwards," Camila said, not unkindly, and Paige was quiet, because she had done the same thing an hour earlier and only erased it out of suspicion, not understanding.

"Think about what the angle means," Camila went on, and then stopped herself. "No, wait, figure it out, that's the rule, Mr. Bui's rule."

The rule was real. Mr. Bui, who lived two doors down and had supposedly retired from teaching but could be lured onto a porch with almost any question, had told Paige in July, when she'd asked whether physics was a mistake, that the way to know a thing was to build it herself and then break it. Sunny, meanwhile, had gotten up and gone to the freezer for ice, holding it against her wrist, claiming an old soccer injury, though everyone knew she just liked the drama of it.

Paige took a fresh sheet. She drew the velocity as an arrow slanting just above the ground, then two more arrows, one flat along the ground and one straight up, and looked at which one was long. At eight degrees, the launch was almost flat, so most of the velocity had to lie along the ground. "The horizontal component is twelve times the cosine of eight degrees," she said slowly, "and the vertical is twelve times the sine. So the vertical part is tiny. Cosine goes with the flat direction, sine goes with the up direction." She checked the numbers: almost twelve meters per second sideways, a little under one and a half up. The ball would skim out low and long, not fountain upward. She turned the sheet toward Sunny, who looked at it, then at her own paper, then said, "So I predicted a ball thrown almost flat would go almost straight up. Great. Wonderful. Put that on my grave."

They worked the rest of the set that way, Sunny demanding a recount at every step, Camila occasionally reading a sentence aloud from her immunology book about things that had no business being mixed with projectile motion, though once, on a break, she said something about how the body decides what is self and what is other, and Paige thought that choosing physics had felt a bit like that, a decision about what she was going to be. She didn't say it aloud. She was still not sure the choice had been right rather than merely hers, and Sunny, refreshed by drama and ice, was already loudly planning a victory celebration involving a slushie, her eligibility, and somebody else's money.

At midnight they stood on the front step while Sunny pointed at the streetlight and asked, gesturing with a pretzel, what angle Paige thought a punt should be, and whether they could calculate it before practice Tuesday. Paige said she thought so, or thought she could find out, which was a different thing, and Sunny said that was good enough for her.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Trade based on comparative advantage raises a country's total income, but individual workers in industries that now face cheaper imports can still lose their jobs or wages.
story:
Sydney had set the lemonade stand up in her driveway with a hand-lettered sign that said FRESH, HONEST, REASONABLY PRICED, which she considered a work of marketing genius until Kierra pointed out it sounded like a used car lot. The three of them, Sydney, Kierra, and Bronson, were supposed to be splitting the work and the profits, but so far the work had mostly consisted of Sydney trying to study while the other two argued about whether the recipe had too much pulp.

"It's a lineage," Kierra said, defending the recipe she had inherited from her grandmother. "You don't just change a lineage. That's like redrawing your family tree because you think your uncle is boring."

"You can't parametrize a lemonade recipe anyway," Bronson said, thumbing through Sydney's economics notes, which she had clipped open with a clothespin because the wind kept trying to steal them. "Wait. Is this what you're being tested on Monday? Comparative advantage? Because I know exactly one thing about that, and it's that my dad says it's why the muffler plant closed."

Sydney put down the pitcher. This was the part she had been circling all week. In the textbook it was clean: two countries, each better at something, both better off if they traded. She could recite it. But on Thursday she had praised free trade at her grandfather's kitchen table, saying trade made countries richer overall, and her grandfather had set down his coffee and asked, very quietly, who exactly the "overall" was, because he'd worked at a battery plant for twenty-six years and the doors had been chained one morning, and he had watched his whole town get good at being unemployed. She hadn't had an answer. She'd said something about efficiency and he'd laughed, not unkindly, and said efficiency was a word people used when the money went somewhere she couldn't see it.

"Okay," Sydney said now, lining up three cups on the folding table. "Kierra, you make better lemonade than Bronson. And you're also better than him at talking customers into buying the overpriced cookies."

"Deeply true," Kierra said.

"And Bronson, you're worse than her at both. But you're less bad at the cookies than at the lemonade, right? Like, if we both had to do everything ourselves, I lose more by making bad lemonade than you lose by selling bad cookies." She was working it out as she said it, the way she hadn't been able to at her grandfather's table. "So even though Kierra's better at everything, if she does lemonade and Bronson does cookies, we make more total than if everybody does their own everything. That's comparative advantage. Both of us come out ahead."

"So the country gets richer," Bronson said. "Great. My dad will be thrilled the country is richer. He was making nineteen dollars an hour at the plant and now he makes eleven at the hardware store, and the country is richer."
