A customer arrived, a woman with a stroller, and Kierra poured while Bronson, who was intransigent about product, offered her a cookie he had personally not touched. The woman paid, said the lemonade was lovely, and rolled on toward the park. Sydney watched the dollar go into the cash box and felt the shape of the problem more clearly than the textbook had ever drawn it. The stand's total money was up. The total was up, and one person's share was down, and both of those things were true at the same time, not one canceling the other out.

"Here's what I think," she said slowly. "I think the book isn't lying. If the whole country's income is bigger after trading, that's real. But so is your dad's four dollars an hour, and so is my grandpa's chained door. It's not that the gains aren't real. It's that they don't go to the people who paid for them." She turned a cup in her hands. "And I don't know what you do about that. I've been trying to figure out whether the two things can both be true without one of them being a trick, and I think they can, and I think that's what I couldn't say to my grandpa."

Bronson was quiet for a second, stacking cookies into a neater pyramid, which was his version of thinking. "You should tell him that," he said. "Not the textbook part. The part where you said the gains don't go to the people who paid for them. He'd like that you said the second half out loud."

"Test's Monday," Kierra said. "Grandpa's Sunday. Tragic scheduling."

Sydney wrote it on the back of the sign in marker, where the wind couldn't get it: TOTAL UP, PEOPLE DOWN, BOTH REAL. Then she picked up the pitcher and refilled Kierra's cup without being asked, because pouring was her worst job of the three, and that, she thought, was probably the whole point.

"Last call," Bronson called down the street. "Honest lemonade, reasonably priced, and free economics lessons with every cup."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Ford Madox Ford's 1915 novel The Good Soldier opens with its narrator, John Dowell, saying, 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard.'
story:
The copy of The Good Soldier that Julia had requested through interlibrary loan arrived on a Thursday, thin and blue-covered, smelling faintly of some other town's shelves. She had signed out the carrel by the periodicals because it faced the window and because hardly anyone sat there after four o'clock, when the light through the glass turned the whole reading room the color of weak tea. Her assignment was to write about point of view, about how a narrator builds or spends the reader's trust, and Mr. Fitzgerald had told the class only this: pick a narrator you don't believe, and figure out when you stopped believing him.

She opened to the first page. "This is the saddest story I have ever heard." She read the sentence twice, then sat very still, because something about it had snagged on her like a sleeve on a nail. Heard, she thought. Not lived. Not suffered. The narrator of the book, a man named John Dowell, was writing about his own marriage, his own wife Florence, his own nine years of a life, and yet he framed it as something that had come to him secondhand, a tale delivered across a table. She checked the publication date on the copyright page, 1915, and wrote in her notebook: he calls it the saddest story he has ever heard, but he was in it.

Jeanne arrived at five with her backpack still on one shoulder and a granola bar she wasn't technically supposed to have in the building. She dropped into the chair across from Julia and peered at the open book upside down.

"That's the one Fitzgerald wouldn't stop talking about," Jeanne said. "The sad saddest story one."

"But listen," Julia said, and read the first line aloud, quietly, because a man two tables over kept glancing over at them whenever their voices rose. "Heard. He heard it. It's his own life."

Jeanne frowned, unwrapping the granola bar with the slow caution of someone defusing something. "Maybe that's just how people talked in 1915."

"Or maybe he doesn't want to own it." Julia turned the book over in her hands, felt the soft worn edges of the cover, the small library stamp faded on the back. "If it happened to him, then he has to admit he was there. He has to admit he didn't see it."

Jeanne chewed and considered, and for a while they worked in a companionable quiet, Julia taking notes, Jeanne pretending to study for chemistry but drifting back to the blue book every few minutes. At one point a librarian passed their table and paused, and Jeanne remonstrated with her silently, pointing at the granola bar with an expression of such theatrical innocence that the librarian laughed under her breath and kept walking.

Julia kept circling the same problem. She had been taught, in every essay she had ever written, to trust the person telling the story. The teacher, the textbook, the narrator. And here was a man insisting on his own sadness while sliding out from under it, sentence by sentence. She thought about her mother, who told the story of the divorce the same way, as something that had happened to the family, a weather event, no one holding the umbrella backwards. There had been a consonance between the way her mother told it and the way Julia wanted to hear it, both of them preferring the version where nobody had chosen anything, and it had taken Julia a year to notice she preferred it too.

She wrote that down, then crossed it out, then wrote it smaller.

"Okay," she said to Jeanne. "So my whole essay is: the narrator is unreliable, and the first sentence tells you so, if you're paying attention. He's not lying about the facts. He's lying about his position."

"Lying is a big word."

"Cooperating with himself, then. Being glacial about it. Moving so slow you don't see the movement."

Jeanne looked at her. "That's actually good. Write that one down."

But walking home later under the streetlights, the book heavy in her bag, Julia wasn't sure she had it settled. Maybe Dowell had earned the right to call his own life something he'd heard; maybe distance was the only mercy available to him. She couldn't decide whether the narrator was a coward or a man performing his grief the only way he could stand to, and she suspected the honest essay was the one that said so. She stopped at the corner by the bakery, took out her notebook, and added a line beneath everything else: I stopped trusting him on the first page, and I don't know yet if that was fair.

A car passed, its headlights sweeping the wet crosswalk. She zipped the bag shut and kept walking.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In 1854, physician John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London and showed they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street, an early example of spatial analysis.
story:
Ashley's laptop had been rendering the flood layer for eleven minutes, and in that time she had eaten a cold piece of toast, refilled her water twice, and watched her brother's cat knock a pencil off the desk with the patience of a professional. The assignment was due Monday. Mr. Park had said, more than once, that a map was an argument, and Ashley was beginning to suspect her argument was that her laptop was garbage.

Marco came over at four with his own laptop under his arm and a bag of the orange crackers he liked, which he ate loudly, on principle. He wanted to build a project on bike lanes, all bike lanes, nothing but bike lanes, and he had decided that helping Ashley with her flood map was a fair trade for her helping him figure out his introduction. "You need a hook," he said, crumbs landing on her keyboard. "Every good project starts with a hook. Mine starts with the year the city paved over the river trail."

"My hook is that half the cheap housing in this city sits inside the flood zone," Ashley said. She turned the laptop toward him. The map had finally loaded: pale streets, and over them a blue wash where the river had historically gone when it stopped behaving. She had spent two evenings digitizing parcels from a scanned plat map, and another hour figuring out how to make the software treat her flood layer and her housing layer as things that could be stacked, each one translucent, so the dark places meant both things at once.

"That's not a hook, that's a bummer," Marco said. He leaned in anyway, chewing more quietly, which for Marco was a form of respect. "Wait. Go back. That triangle of streets by the viaduct."

She zoomed. The blue wash covered it completely, and under the blue, the parcels she had coded as low-income came up dark, almost black, an amalgam of two datasets neither of which said anything about the other until she put them on top of each other. Then they said a lot. She sat back. Outside, her mother was arguing with the barbecue, which had been atrophying in the garage since her father left and had finally been dragged out for one last season.

"You need the introduction tonight," Marco said. He had his own reasons for nagging; his bike lane project had stalled at paragraph one and he was hoping that if Ashley found her opening, some of it would rub off on him. "Tell me you have something."

"I have the Broad Street thing," she said. "From the article Mr. Park linked. In 1854, this physician, John Snow, mapped cholera deaths in London. He plotted where people died on a street map, and the deaths clustered around one water pump, the one on Broad Street. It's basically the first spatial analysis. Nobody had to understand the disease. They could see it on the map."

"Wait, that's it?" Marco was already typing it into his own document under Bike Lanes, A History. "Some guy draws dots and the dots mean something?"

"That's the whole idea, yes. You look at where, not just how many. Where the deaths were was the answer." She paused. "Or the beginning of one. They took the handle off the pump." She said it lightly, but she was thinking about her black triangle, about whether seeing it clearly was the same as being able to do anything about it, about whether a map that showed a problem was a promise or just a picture of one. She didn't say any of that out loud, partly because she wasn't sure, and partly because Marco had found the crackers again.

He stayed for another hour, and between his commentary he actually helped, suggesting she use a graduated color ramp for the housing values so the flood overlap would read at a glance instead of requiring the squinting her current version demanded. It worked. By six the map looked like something a person would stop and look at, the blue and the dark lying over the city together, unhurried, as if they had always meant to be seen that way. Marco packed up his laptop, still without his introduction, and said he would text her the Broad Street wording he'd stolen so she could check that he hadn't mangled it.

After he left, Ashley sat with the map full screen. Her mother called through the window that the barbecue had won again and they were ordering pizza. On the screen, the triangle by the viaduct sat there, dark and patient, waiting for Monday. She saved the file, then saved it again somewhere else.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Thomas Carlyle's The French Revolution: A History, published in 1837, stressed the moral choices of individuals rather than impersonal historical forces.
story:
Coralie had reserved a table in the city archive's rare reading room, which meant she was allowed one pencil, one notebook, and no opinions out loud. The essay was due in three weeks: how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. Ms. Njoroge had warned the class against inventing a tidy line of progress. "Historians disagree," she had said, "and your job is to map the disagreement, not to referee it." Coralie had nodded then, but now, facing her notebook's blank first page, she wanted a referee badly.

She started with the cart of reserved volumes, and the second one stopped her. Thomas Carlyle, The French Revolution: A History, published in 1837. She knew the name from a lecture slide, one line in a list, but the book itself was something else. Her grandfather's copy, she realized, checking the bookplate, the one she had struggled through at his house last spring, arguing with his truculent marginalia in the margins. Danton, Mirabeau, the fall of the Bastille, all of it written like thunder. She opened to her own faint pencil marks from that visit, when she had been taking notes and had written, frustrated, in the margin of her notebook, "how does anyone cite this."

Treyton slid into the chair across from her, wearing his archive lanyard from the volunteer desk, and set down his phone. "Cooper says you're doing the historiography thing," he said. "He wants your secondary-source list. He also wants to know if you failed at Carlyle like he did."

"Nobody fails at Carlyle," Coralie said. "It's not that kind of book." She turned pages for him, dramatic ones, the prose rolling like a speech. "Look. He keeps making it turn on people. Danton chooses, Robespierre chooses, the King chooses. Whether they choose well or badly."

"Isn't that just how old books wrote?" Treyton said. "Before they got scientific about it?"

That was the question, and Coralie felt it land somewhere real. Later that afternoon, in the archive's common room, she found Cooper hunched over a Marxist survey from the 1960s, its argument dense and certain, everything turning on forces, classes, structures that moved individuals whether they liked it or not. He showed her a passage and she set Carlyle beside it on the table, two books open like two witnesses who could not agree on what kind of event they had even seen.

That evening her grandfather emailed, because he refused to text. "I hear from your mother you are wrestling with my Carlyle. I would not dream of rescuing you. But when I was your age I believed the book, all of it, and only later did I learn that believing an author is not the same as testing him. Write to me what you decide. I will argue either side. G." Coralie read it twice. He was not offering help; he was offering an opponent, which from him was a kind of love, and also a dare. She noticed what he had not said: not "Carlyle was right," only that he had once believed it. Something in his certainty, she suspected, had calcified long ago and he knew it.

She drafted the essay in the archive's quiet room over two Saturdays. The middle paragraphs came easily, the contrast between Carlyle's moral drama and the structural accounts that came after. The harder part was the ending, because her honest conclusion was not that one side won. People making choices mattered; forces larger than people also mattered; each generation of historians seemed to lean one way and then the other, and she could not prove which lean was correct. She wrote a paragraph claiming Carlyle's approach had been superseded, read it, and crossed it out, because it was not true, and Ms. Njoroge would know it was not true, and worse, she would know it herself.

She kept instead a paragraph that ended, "Carlyle published his history in 1837, and its insistence that individuals' moral choices, not impersonal historical forces, drove the Revolution has never been fully answered, only rephrased." Then she added a sentence admitting that she did not know whether the rephrasings were progress or fashion. Ms. Njoroge's comment, when the draft came back, ran along the bottom in green ink: "This is the first essay this term that stays honest at the point where it gets hard. Come see me about footnotes."

On the last Saturday before the deadline, Coralie returned the Carlyle to the reserve cart. Her grandfather's bookplate, she noticed, had her name in pencil beneath his, added at some point without an announcement, the way he did things. She photographed the open title page and sent him one line with it: "I decided it's a book you argue with, not a book you settle." Then she signed out at the front desk, took her pencil back from the guard, and walked out into the ordinary daylight where nobody was making history, or everybody was.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together.
story:
The house had no curtains yet, so the morning light came in without manners, laying itself across the bare floor of Florence's room in long white bars. She sat on the floor with her back against a cardboard box marked SCHOOL STUFF, phone in her lap, and watched Maite's name on the screen without pressing it. Three time zones sat between here and home. It was still early there, probably, and Maite would still be asleep in a town where the mountains were just mountains, not the flattened, montane silhouettes this new city stacked along its horizon like a backdrop nobody had bothered to paint properly.

Downstairs, her mother was measuring the kitchen for curtains, unspooling the tape measure with a sound like a small machine. Florence could hear her verbalize every number as she went, a habit from her job, forty-two and a half, sixty-one even, and Florence found it almost comforting, the way arithmetic filled an empty house.

She called Maite anyway.

"You're up early," Maite said, voice thick with sleep.

"It's later here. Everything's later here." Florence pulled her knees in. "I read something. This study. A guy named Jeffrey Hall, 2018. He estimated it takes more than 200 hours spent together to become close friends."

"Hours?"

"Together. Like actually together, in the same room, doing stuff."

There was a pause, the kind that carried a whole second meaning in it. "Is that supposed to make me feel better or worse?"

"Both. Maybe. I did the math on us." Florence picked at the tape on the box beside her. "Seven years. Lunch every school day, plus weekends, plus the summer at the pool. I stopped counting past 200 in about a year and a half. We had, like, thousands."

"So we're safe."

"I don't know. That's hours becoming friends. Nobody studied the hours for keeping them." She heard herself say it and couldn't take it back, and it hung there.

"Flo." Maite's voice flattened. "Are you saying you think this fades?"

"No. I'm saying I don't know what I'm saying."

They talked for six more minutes about Maite's aunt's wedding and a rumor about Logan and a girl from the swim team, and then Maite said her mom needed the phone, which her mom never needed, and Florence said okay, and they hung up on the word okay, both of them, at the same time, which used to be a thing they did for fun.

She sat with the phone a while. Then she got up and walked through the empty house in her socks, the sound enormous in the hollow rooms. Her mother stood in the kitchen doorway with the tape measure draped around her neck like a scarf. "You hate it here," her mother said. Not a question.

"It's a confounder," Florence said. "Everything I feel about the house is mixed up with everything I feel about leaving. I can't separate them."

Her mother considered this. "You sound like your father."

Later that afternoon the doorbell rang, which was strange, because the doorbell had a cardboard sign taped over it that said DO NOT USE, WORKING ON IT. Florence opened the door anyway. A woman stood on the concrete step holding a casserole dish covered in foil, and behind her a girl about Florence's age hovered at the edge of the porch, pretending to be interested in the moving truck.

"I'm Ms. Okonkwo, from two doors down. You're the new family." She passed over the dish. "This is my niece, staying with me for the summer. She's been complaining there's no one under forty on this street."

"I wasn't complaining," the girl said. "I was observing."

Florence stepped back from the door. "You can come in. There's nowhere to sit, but you can come in."

They ended up on the kitchen floor with the casserole between them, eating straight from the dish with forks because every plate was still boxed. The girl, whose name was Logan, was staying the summer only, then going back to her own city, and she said this in the flat way of someone who had already decided the summer didn't matter.

"Two months," Logan said, sawing at a corner of the casserole. "Then gone. What's the point of starting anything."

Florence thought about the 200 hours, the careful arithmetic of closeness, the study that measured how friendships get built but not how they break. "Two months is a lot of hours," she said. "If you count them."

"Counting doesn't make people stay."

"No," Florence agreed. "It doesn't."

They ate in silence for a minute, and then Logan asked if any of the boxes had board games in them, and Florence said probably, and got up to go look.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: In Westminster-style parliaments, the third reading is the final debate and vote on a bill as amended, after its details have been examined in committee.
story:
The bus smelled of cherry cough drops, and Alyssa had eaten three of them before the legislature came into view, sandstone and green copper, a building that took itself seriously. Mr. Luo counted them twice in the rotunda, under a marble man holding a scroll, and said, "Remember, you're here as members, not tourists," which was rich, since half of them were photographing the chandeliers.

They had been assigned a model parliament, each student a member with a bill to shepherd. Alyssa's bill proposed free transit passes for impecunious students, which was a word she had put in the first line mostly to annoy Dakota, who said it made the bill sound like it needed a translator. It had survived drafting, when Mr. Luo had made her strike four clauses she couldn't defend. It had survived committee, barely, after Savanah's committee had amended it so the passes were means-tested, which Alyssa had hated, then accepted, then quietly liked, because a bill that passed with a flaw in it was still a bill that passed.

"It's not a betrayal," Savanah had told her in the hallway, adjusting the sash she'd made that said COMMITTEE CHAIR in duct tape letters. "It's a compromise. That's literally the job."

"I wanted it clean," Alyssa said.

"Clean bills die in committee. You can visit their graves on the way out."

Now they filed into the visitors' gallery, then down onto the floor of a chamber that was mostly empty, the real members elsewhere, the clerks amused. Mr. Luo took the Speaker's chair with the reluctance of a man who had been asked to do this before and had learned not to enjoy it. "We proceed to third reading," he said. "The final debate and vote on the bill as amended, after the committee's examination. Members, the floor is open."

Dakota leaned across the aisle. "What does that mean, as amended?"

"It means my original bill is dead," Alyssa said. "What's alive is the version they changed. If it passes, that's the version that passes, means-testing and all."

"So debate it or lose it."

She stood. The room was smaller than the rotunda had implied, and her voice hit the wood panelling and came back at her. She argued the bill was still worth passing, that the committee's amendment was not a wound but scar tissue, proof the thing had survived contact with people who disagreed. She heard herself making Savanah's argument in her own sentences, and it didn't feel like surrender. It felt like she had turned the problem over enough times to see it had two defensible faces, and she'd stopped pretending it had one.

Dakota rose against it, because Dakota liked being an iconoclast and had once told her, with pride, that he'd argued against his own birthday party on procedural grounds. He called the means test bureaucratic, a form for a bus ticket, a fence around a bench. It was a good speech. Alyssa found herself nodding at parts of it, which Dakota noticed, and which he later claimed to find insulting.

The debate went around the room. A boy from another school wanted to know the cost, and no one could tell him, and Mr. Luo said members were not required to be accountants, which settled nothing and everybody. A girl argued that students who could afford fares should pay them, fairness spoken like a fact. Savanah argued the amended bill would reach more of the students who actually needed it than the pure version would have, and Alyssa watched her own earlier position get dismantled by the person who had forced it on her in the first place.

They voted by standing. Alyssa stood. Dakota stayed seated, arms folded, but he was looking at her, not at the bill, and he mouthed something that might have been "good speech" or might have been "sellout," and possibly he didn't know which himself. The count came out fourteen to nine, and Mr. Luo, in the Speaker's chair, announced that the bill had passed third reading and would now receive assent. He produced, from beneath the desk, a plastic sceptre from the dollar store, held it over the paper with tremendous gravity, and said, "Assented."

Everyone applauded. Savanah applauded hardest, because the committee's amendment was now, technically, law, and she had engineered it. Alyssa sat down holding her amended bill, the paper warm from being passed along the rows, and read the means-testing clause again, the one she'd fought and then defended and then, in the debate, actually meant.

Afterward, in the rotunda, Dakota caught up with her under the marble man with the scroll. "You know they're going to lionize you for this," he said. "Savanah's already telling people from the other school it was her bill."

"It was her amendment."

"Same thing, apparently." He looked at the marble man. "For what it's worth, I voted no because of the fence around the bench. Not because of you."

"I know."

"Also I kind of wanted your version. The clean one." He shrugged. "Somebody has to want the clean one, or nobody ever drafts it."

Mr. Luo was collecting sashes near the door, folding Savanah's COMMITTEE CHAIR into his bag with the sceptre. Alyssa folded her bill and put it in her back pocket, where it would go through the wash and come out a soft grey brick, though she didn't know that yet. What she knew was that the version that passed wasn't the one she'd written, and she couldn't decide whether that was the system working or the price of it, and Dakota was holding out his hand, so she shook it.

"Fence around the bench," she said. "I'm stealing that."

"Too late," said Dakota. "It's already amended."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Modus ponens is the valid argument form 'if P then Q; P; therefore Q', and it is valid no matter what P and Q stand for.
story:
Rosalie arrived at the library twenty minutes early because the practice exam was on Saturday and her scholarship interview was on Monday and she had promised her mother she would stop guessing her way through the logic section. She spread the booklet on the table by the window, where the late light fell across the page, and read the sample question for the third time. If the blorx is midge, then the plen is frobe. The blorx is midge. What follows?

"That's the stupidest thing I've ever read," said Carla, dropping into the chair across from her with a stack of her own books. "They can't test us on words that don't exist."

"It's not about the words," Rosalie said, but she wasn't sure what it was about, which was the problem. She copied the argument onto a fresh sheet. If the blorx is midge, then the plen is frobe. The blorx is midge. Therefore the plen is frobe. She wrote it and stared at it, waiting to feel something click, and nothing clicked. She tried replacing the nonsense with something real. If it rains, the match is cancelled. It rains. The match is cancelled. That worked, obviously. She went back to the blorx. It worked there too, in the same way, and she sat with her pen hovering because she could not yet say why.

Edmond appeared with two granola bars and no greeting, which was his way. He read over her shoulder for a moment. "Mr. Robinson gave us that form last term," he said. "If P then Q; P; therefore Q. It's called modus ponens." He tore open a granola bar. "It's valid no matter what P and Q stand for. That's the whole point of the nonsense words."

"You could put anything in it," Carla said. "If my grandmother is a toaster, then the moon is made of homework. My grandmother is a toaster. Therefore the moon is made of homework."

"Therefore the moon is made of homework," Rosalie repeated, and laughed despite herself, and then stopped laughing because something had shifted. The argument was ridiculous and it held. She wrote Carla's version out in the P and Q pattern and it looked exactly like the rain argument, exactly like the blorx argument, and the shape was doing all the work while the words did none. "It doesn't care whether anything is true," she said slowly. "It only cares about the fit."

Mr. Robinson passed their table on his way to the returns cart and paused long enough to see her page. "Practice exam?" he said. She nodded, and he only said, "Saturday, ten o'clock, don't be late," and moved on. That was typical of him. He would never explain anything at a table; he believed explaining robbed you of the discovery, which Rosalie had found infuriating in September and found, now, less so.

She tried to break the form. If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q. She tested it with rain. If it rains, the match is cancelled. It doesn't rain. Therefore the match is not cancelled. But the match could be cancelled for other reasons, she realized, a burst pipe, a fight between the coaches, and the argument had gone quietly wrong somewhere. She crossed it out. The form from the booklet held where this one failed, and the difference between them was not in the words at all, both used rain, both used the match, but in the arrangement. She felt the turgid weight of the practice booklet lift slightly, or perhaps not lift but redistribute, the way a heavy thing becomes manageable once you know where to grip it.

Carla had gone quiet, chewing her pen, ruminate written all over her face. "So on Saturday they could give us anything," she said. "Total garbage words, and we just have to see the shape under them."

"That's the substrate," Edmond said. "The words are sitting on top of the structure. Take the words away, the structure's still there." He said it while looking at his granola bar, not at her, as though it were an unremarkable fact about the bar.

Rosalie copied the blorx argument one more time, cleanly, and then rewrote it with P and Q, and then once more with the rain, three arguments in a column, the same skeleton showing through each of them. On Monday the interviewers would ask her why she wanted the scholarship, and she had rehearsed an answer about curiosity, and she had suspected until now that it was a rehearsed thing, a costume. Sitting here with the nonsense words, she was less sure it was a costume. Something in her wanted the shape under the blorx, and had wanted it before she had a name for it, and she could admit that without knowing whether it would survive her actually getting the scholarship or losing it. That part stayed open. She underlined the column of arguments and put a box around it, then packed her bag while Carla copied her page in fast, sideways handwriting.

"Ten o'clock Saturday," Carla said. "Bring the grandmother toaster one. I want to see their faces."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Charlotte had spent forty minutes choosing between two shirts, and the winner, a thin green thing her mother called flattering, now clung to her back with sweat in the bowling alley's fluorescent heat. The boy, whom she had met exactly once, at a friend's party where they had talked for eleven minutes about a documentary neither of them had finished, was unlacing his borrowed shoes at lane fourteen. He looked up when she approached and stood so quickly he knocked the score sheet off the console, and she caught it, which felt like the first thing she had done right all evening.

"You bowl?" he asked.

"I've bowled," she said, which was technically true of a ninth-grade birthday party she had mostly spent at the snack bar. He nodded as though this were a real answer, and entered her name into the screen with two fingers, hunting each letter.

Her first ball went into the gutter. So did her second. He didn't laugh, or he laughed only a little, in a way she couldn't read, and she thought about Ayanna, who read psychology articles the way other people read horoscopes, and who had cornered her at lunch on Thursday. "There's this thing called the liking gap," Ayanna had said, apropos of nothing, apropos of everything. "This study, 2018, Erica Boothby and colleagues. After a first conversation, people underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. Everybody does it. You'll do it too."

"I'm not nervous," Charlotte had said, which was a lie so obvious that Ayanna had simply handed her a tangerine and changed the subject.

The boy, whose own bowling was competent and unshowy, fetched her a lemonade without being asked. She watched him carry it back across the carpet, that sedimentary carpet, layered with decades of spilled soda and ground-in popcorn, and she thought about the veneer of composure she was maintaining, how thin it was, how it could survive a gutter ball but maybe not a second one. She thanked him. He said, "You hold it like it's a bird," and she looked down and saw that she was cradling the cup with both hands, and laughed before she could stop herself.

After that it got easier, or it got different. He told her about his younger sister's obsession with competitive jump-roping, an entire subculture he described in baffled, affectionate detail, and Charlotte told him about the summer she and Koralie had tried to run a lawn-mowing business and netted eleven dollars. He asked a follow-up question about Koralie, which almost nobody did. On her fifth frame she knocked down eight pins, and she did a small, involuntary gesture with her fists, and he clapped twice, and she felt something invigorate her, some part of the evening that had been sitting inert.

They tied. Neither of them had planned to, and neither would admit to caring, but they recounted the scores twice, and he won the recount on a technicality involving her tenth-frame gutter, and they argued about the technicality all the way to the counter, where he paid for the shoes before she could get her wallet out, and she said, "Next time," and heard the words leave her mouth like a bird she hadn't meant to release.

The trouble was the walk. He went left at the parking lot, toward the bus stop, and she went right, and the farther she got from the building the more the whole evening rearranged itself against her. The eleven-minute party conversation, she decided, had been the real evidence, and tonight was contaminated; he had laughed at the wrong moments, or the right moments but too politely; he'd paid because he wanted to leave quickly and cleanly, no debts outstanding; the follow-up question about Koralie was filler, the sort of thing you asked to keep a dying evening on its feet. By the time she reached her block she had the whole autopsy done, the evening opened and labeled. He had hated it. He had tolerated it. He had enjoyed her company the way you enjoy a delayed flight, by making the best of it.

She was halfway up the front steps when she checked her phone, more out of habit than hope. There was a text, sent four minutes ago. "this is going to sound like a lie but that was the most fun I've had in months. also I checked and the technicality was real, you owe me a rematch." She stood on the steps holding the phone with both hands, like it was a bird, and the careful case she had built against herself did not collapse so much as sit there, waiting for her to decide what to do with it. She typed, deleted, typed again. "rematch is accepted. but I'm bringing a ringer." Then she stood in the dark a moment longer, watching the screen, until the three dots appeared.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A getter that returns a reference to a private mutable object, such as a list, lets outside code change it, so programmers often return a copy instead.
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm dust and lemon cleaner, and the radiators clanked in a rhythm Violet had begun to think of as the building's leitmotif, the one sound that followed her through every late afternoon of her final spring. She had claimed the machine in the corner, the one whose monitor flickered if you bumped the desk, and she had been there for an hour before Sidney arrived, sliding into the next seat with a bag of pretzels and no apology.

"Did you finish the playlist assignment?" Sidney asked, though she could see the screen well enough. "Ms. Cruz wants a class with private fields. Getters. A test."

"I'm building a Playlist class," Violet said. "Private field for the songs, a list of strings. Getter called getSongs. It compiles."

Sidney leaned over and typed a few lines in her own file, in the main method of a separate class, the way the assignment required: create a Playlist, call the getter, print what came back. It worked on Sidney's machine. On Violet's, the test was longer, a loop that checked the size of the list before and after something else ran, and it was already failing when Sidney looked at it.

"It says your playlist has zero songs," Sidney said. "You added six."

Violet scrolled. She had added six. The constructor filled the list with six titles, and the toString printed all of them, and the test had passed at three o'clock. She said so, and Sidney shrugged and started eating pretzels again, and Lohan came in from the hallway with snow on his shoulders and a theory that the lab machines were haunted. He had failed a keyboarding test in this room in tenth grade and had denigrated the equipment ever since, every projector, every mouse, with the conviction of someone collecting evidence for an old grievance.

"Run it again," Lohan said, dragging a chair over. "Maybe it's the flicker."

She ran it again. Six songs printed. Then the test ran, the one in the other class, the one Ms. Cruz had written on the board as a model and told them to copy into a file of their own. Add the songs. Print. Then something. Then print again. Violet had typed the middle part from memory and hadn't looked at it since, because it was three lines and she had been thinking about the train schedule, about whether she could still catch the 5:40 if she stayed another twenty minutes.

The output came up. Six songs. Then three lines of the test doing whatever it did. Then the second print: empty brackets, the melancholic punctuation of a list with nothing in it.

"Zero," Lohan said. "There it is again."

Sidney stopped chewing. Nobody said anything for a moment, and Violet felt the particular quiet of a room in which three people are all waiting for someone else to be wrong first. She clicked open the test file and scrolled to the middle, to the three lines she had trusted, and read them slowly, the way Ms. Cruz had told them to read code that worked yesterday. The first line called getSongs and stored the result in a variable in the test class. The second line called clear on that variable. The third line printed the playlist.

"You emptied it," Sidney said. "From over there. But the field's private."

"It is private," Violet said. Her voice came out flat, and she heard herself sounding like her father denying a plumbing problem, and she stopped. She looked at the getter she had written, the one line that returned the list itself, songs, no copies, no questions. The field was private. The getter handed back the actual list, not a description of it, and whatever held it could do anything to it.

"So outside code can still change it," Lohan said slowly, testing the idea the way you test ice.

"Some programmers return a copy instead," Sidney said, already typing it into her own file, defensive, as if the thought belonged to her. "I read that somewhere. A getter that hands out the list itself lets anyone change your private stuff, so you give them a copy." She said it and then looked uneasy, as though the words were bigger in the air than they had been in her head.

Violet changed one line. The getter now built a new list, put the songs in it, and returned that. She ran the test again. Six songs, the clear, six songs. The empty brackets were gone. She sat back and looked at the two versions side by side in her notes, the safe one and the leak, and could not decide which had been the stranger feeling: watching her private list emptied from a class that had no right to it, or learning that privacy in this language was a promise the getter had to keep on its own.

Ms. Cruz came through on her way to the printer, glanced at the screen, and said only, "Fix that in your notes too, not just your code." Then she was gone, pages in hand, and the radiator clanked twice.

"Copy for the test, original for us," Lohan said, and reached past Violet to steal a pretzel.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In the United States, a 100-year flood zone does not mean a flood every 100 years; it means the area has a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year.
story:
The travel agency sat between a nail salon and a closed battery shop, and by the third week of July Jaxon had memorized the smell of it, toner and old carpet and the lemongrass candle Mr. Wong lit in the afternoons when the fan stopped being enough. His job was simple: answer the phone, update the brochure rack, enter package prices into the booking system. But Mr. Wong had also let him bring his laptop to the back counter, and that was where Jaxon spent the slow hours teaching himself the mapping software his cousin Gwyneth had shown him in June, the kind planners used, where you could stack layers of a city on top of each other like sheets of glass.

He was doing it for his mother. She had found a listing in the east part of the city, a small yellow house with a fenced yard, and the seller's agent had sent her a note that read, in part, Wonderful news: the property is only in the 100-year flood zone, so you are safe for a century. His mother had taped the note to the refrigerator and started packing boxes in her head. Jaxon had looked at the sentence for a long time before something about it bothered him, though he could not yet say what.

"The flood layer goes on top of the parcels," Gwyneth said on the Tuesday she came in, sliding onto the stool beside him with her backpack still on one shoulder. She had stopped by after her shift at the library, and she drank the iced tea Mr. Wong brought her without being asked, which was the kind of small thing Mr. Wong did for everyone and never mentioned. "Tint it light. If you make it opaque you can't see the streets underneath."

Jaxon clicked the layer into place. The city appeared as it really was: a pale wash of blue-green spread across the eastern flats, swallowing whole blocks, and inside it, when he zoomed, a small yellow polygon with a fence around its edge in the satellite photo. His mother's house. Gwyneth leaned in and said nothing for a moment, which he understood as its own kind of statement.

He printed the map and folded it into his pocket, and that evening Kelly from his econ class came by the agency to pick up brochures for her family's trip and ended up sitting across from him while he explained it. "The agent says a hundred years," Kelly said. "Sounds solid."

"It sounded solid to me too." Jaxon pulled up the county's flood page on the laptop and turned it so she could read. "But a 100-year flood zone does not mean a flood every 100 years. It means the area has a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year."

Kelly frowned. "One percent. That's nothing."

"Every year," Jaxon said. "It doesn't reset. And it doesn't add up the way you'd think either, honestly, I'm still working out what it adds up to. Over thirty years of a mortgage, the chance is a lot more than one percent. I did the multiplication at two in the morning." He rubbed his eyes. "The bigger problem is I don't know how old the map is. The lines get drawn from old data, and I can't tell from here whether the creek was rerouted or whether the new culvert changed anything. So I know the zone. I don't know how much to trust the zone."

When Mr. Wong came over, drying his hands on a dish towel, Jaxon expected him to talk about flood insurance, which is what Mr. Wong talked about whenever the subject of water came near his shop, since his brother's store had gone under in a spring storm years before and the insurance had moved at a glacial pace while the inventory molded. Instead Mr. Wong looked at the map for a while and said, "Your mother wants this house very much, yes?"

"She's been looking for two years," Jaxon said. "This is the first one she can afford."

Mr. Wong nodded slowly. "Then don't take her hope away with a picture. Take her the picture and the questions. There is a difference." He set a fresh cup of tea beside Kelly's empty glass, then stood there a moment longer, as if deciding whether to say the rest. "When my brother argued with the adjusters, he wanted me to tell him it would be fine. I told him the truth instead, and it hurt him. But he made his plans with his eyes open, and that, he told me later, was worth more."

Jaxon thought about how easily his mother's hope could ossify into a decision, how the packed boxes in her head would harden before he could get the words out right. On Thursday she came to the agency after work, still in her uniform, and he sat her down at the back counter and turned the laptop toward her. He showed her the blue-green wash first, then the yellow polygon inside it, then the county page with the words 1 percent chance in any given year, and he let her read it herself, silently, twice.

"Safe for a century," she said finally, tapping the seller's note she had brought along in her purse, as though it might answer for itself.

"That's not what it means," Jaxon said. "And I don't know everything about it either. But I can come with you Saturday to the open house, and we can ask about the map, and about insurance, and about what the neighbors say happens when it rains hard." He reached over and turned the laptop so the two of them could see the map together, the little yellow house floating in all that pale blue-green, and his mother put her hand flat on the screen, right over the yard with the fence.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Kwanzaa, created by Maulana Karenga in 1966, runs from December 26 to January 1 and honors seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja, meaning unity.
story:
The community hall smelled of fried plantains and floor wax, and Lauren stood at the folding table near the kitchen door holding a stack of paper cups like they were a live grenade. Her grandmother had volunteered her for the fifth night of Kwanzaa, then her aunt had amended it to the first night, and nobody had told Lauren what either job actually involved until ten minutes ago, when her grandmother pressed a laminated card into her hand and said, "You'll do the explanation, baby. The young ones should hear it from a young one."

The card was smudged. She could make out a candle diagram and the word Ujima, or possibly Ujima with a coffee stain over the second syllable, and she decided, in the way of someone who would rather improvise than admit confusion, that the first principle was probably Ujima. Community. Responsibility. She had half a memory of it from a school assembly three years ago, which was exactly the kind of memory that incapacitated a person at the worst moment, because it felt like knowledge while behaving like fog.

Megan found her by the punch bowl, wearing a green dress and the expression of someone who had already located the exits. "How bad is it?" Megan asked. "You look like you're about to recite something."

"I might be reciting the wrong thing."

"That's very you."

"Thank you for your support." Lauren flipped the card over. The back was blank, which felt personal. Across the hall, Mohamed-Amine was setting up the kinara on a card table, adjusting each candle with the phlegmatic care of a boy who had done this at his mosque's interfaith night and regarded all candle-related tasks as beneath drama. He caught her looking and gave her a thumbs up so leisurely it could have been mistaken for a wave.

Then the room shifted, or rather her place in it did, and Megan saw the whole thing from the outside for a moment: Lauren walking to the front with the smudged card, the crowd of aunties and toddlers and one very old man in a kufi who had already begun nodding before anything was said. Megan moved to the back, near the folding chairs, close enough to heckle quietly and far enough to deny involvement.

"Um," Lauren said. "Tonight is the first night of Kwanzaa, which was created by Maulana Karenga in 1966. It runs from December 26 to January 1, and it honors seven principles, one each day." That part came out steady, a raft she could stand on. "And the first principle is..." She looked at the card. The stain looked back. She had a choice between guessing and asking, and she thought of her grandmother's face, and then, strangely, of Mr. Cruz, who ran the hall and had spent twenty minutes earlier helping them untangle the extension cords while insisting the cords were not an encumbrance, just badly raised. He had asked a question instead of pretending. "Actually," Lauren said, "does anyone want to say it? I think I learned it wrong."

A woman in the second row, a stranger with a baby on her hip, laughed. "Umoja," she said. "Unity. First day, always."

"Umoja," Lauren repeated. "Unity." The old man in the kufi nodded so hard his chair complained. Mohamed-Amine, from the kinara, called out, "She tested us on purpose," and Lauren bowed, and the baby on the stranger's hip applauded with both hands, which nobody could pretend was for anyone else.

Afterward her grandmother found her by the dessert table. "You asked them."

"I panicked."

"You asked them. That's what Umoja is for, you know. Not the asking. The answering. Somebody in that room knew, and they told you, and now you know." Her grandmother took a cupcake and examined it with suspicion. "Tomorrow is Kujichagulia. Don't volunteer."

"Too late," Megan said, arriving with two cookies and handing one over like a subpoena. "She already did."

Lauren bit the cookie and looked at the kinara, one candle lit, six waiting, the whole week laid out ahead of her like a syllabus she hadn't read. "What's Kujichagulia mean?" she asked.

"Self-determination," said the woman with the baby, passing by with her coat on. "You'll want to memorize that one before somebody tests you again."

"Or," Mohamed-Amine said, raising his cup of punch, "she could just ask."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under English common law, consideration must have some value but need not be a fair price; courts do not generally judge whether a bargain was a good one.
story:
The gym closed at nine, and the clock behind the front desk said 8:41, which gave Gabrielle nineteen minutes to finish the membership paperwork she had been avoiding all week. She stood at the counter with a clipboard, a pen chained to it, and Ms. Nguyen on the other side, tapping a form that was longer than Gabrielle had expected. "Initial here, here, and here," Ms. Nguyen said, sliding her finger down the page. "Terms and conditions on the back, liability waiver on page three, and we need a parent's signature since you're under eighteen."

Gabrielle's mother was in the parking lot, on the phone, insouciant about the whole enterprise, waving a hand that meant five more minutes. Gabrielle read while she waited. The words had a way of stacking up: indemnify, assumption of risk, binding agreement. She had thought joining a gym meant paying money and lifting things, but the form wanted her consent to a small taxonomy of clauses, each with its own heading, as if danger came in distinct species that had to be catalogued one by one.

Behind her, Aaryan was pacing the rubber floor by the water fountain, still in his school jacket, phone in his hand. "I sold my bike," he said, not quite to her. "The good one. The one my dad got me."

"I know the bike," Gabrielle said.

"Fifty dollars. To Alvin's cousin." He said it fast, the way people say things they want to have already said. "He's leaving the country tomorrow morning, taking it with him on the truck. I texted him I want it back and he said a deal's a deal." Aaryan looked at her, and then past her at Ms. Nguyen. "You're a business person. Tell me there's a way."

Ms. Nguyen did not look up from the register. "Did he pay you the fifty?"

"Took it out of his wallet right there. I didn't even sign anything."

"That doesn't matter." Ms. Nguyen counted out change for the last customer of the night. "You offered, he accepted, he paid. That's consideration. It doesn't have to be a fair price, it just has to have some value. Courts don't judge whether you made a good bargain."

Gabrielle stopped reading the liability waiver. "So because it was fifty instead of, what, four hundred, that changes nothing?"

"Nothing," Ms. Nguyen said. "Consideration must have some value, but the court isn't going to tell you whether the bargain was a good one. That part is yours to live with." She said it without cruelty, the way she might announce the pool hours.

Aaryan sat down on the bench by the desk and put his face in his hands. Gabrielle watched him, and she was aware of watching him, aware that some part of her wanted to excoriate him for selling a bike worth hundreds for the price of a dinner, and another part remembered his father had been out of work since spring, remembered the fifty dollars probably mattered more than the principle. She thought about the form under her own hands, all its clauses about what she agreed to and what she gave up. Her signature was going to mean something whether she read every line or none of them, and nobody was going to rescue her from a bad bargain later, either.

The clock said 8:52. Her mother came through the glass doors with the cold still on her coat, and Ms. Nguyen slid the form around for the parent signature. "We close at nine," Ms. Nguyen said, capping her pen afterward and resting it on the counter. "Read it or don't, but once you both sign, it's done."

Aaryan stood up. He looked smaller than he had at 8:41. "The truck leaves at six a.m.," he said. "If I'm going to talk to Alvin's cousin face to face, it has to be tonight."

Gabrielle signed her name at the bottom of the page, the pen dragging on the last letter, and heard the front door chime as her mother stepped back out. Then Aaryan was at the door too, holding it open, waiting to see if she would come with him.

"I don't know what you're going to say to him," she said, gathering her bag.

"Neither do I." He glanced back once at Ms. Nguyen, who had already begun stacking towels behind the desk. "But a deal's a deal isn't the last word. Maybe it's just the first one."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: For an accurate reading, a person should sit quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the arm supported at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers.
story:
Alexis found the cuff in the back of the kitchen drawer, wedged between a dead battery and a takeout menu from a restaurant that had closed two years ago, and he held it up like evidence. His father had been told at his checkup to keep an eye on his numbers, and had responded by buying a machine and then never opening the box, which struck Alexis as a very particular kind of optimism. His mother had signed Alexis up for a health elective that started in September, the one Ms. Nakamura taught, and Alexis figured he could walk into the first class already knowing something. He wanted that. He was tired of being the person who nodded along.

He read the manual at the kitchen table, feet up on a chair, and took his own reading immediately, arm dangling somewhere near his ribs, and the machine flashed a number that made his eyebrows climb. He texted Bently a photo of it. "Am I dying?" Bently replied with a single crying-laughing face and the words "my uncle had that, he was fine, also he was sitting on a couch, where were you."

The next morning Alexis walked to the pharmacy on Sycamore with Bently, mostly for the company and partly because Bently claimed the machine there was superior, though he could not say in what way. Ruth was already loitering by the blood pressure kiosk, eating the last of a bag of sour candies, and she dared Alexis to run a lap around the aisles and then measure himself, "for science." He did it, jogged past the toothpaste and the birthday cards, slid into the seat, and got another alarming number, higher than the kitchen one.

"See, dying," he said.

Ruth leaned against the counter, sucking a candy thoughtfully against her tooth. She said her grandmother's nurse had a whole ritual with the machine, sitting first, and that the nurse had once scolded her for crossing her legs during it. Alexis, still catching his breath, pulled out his phone and looked up how to take a reading properly, and there it was in plain language: for an accurate reading, a person should sit quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the arm supported at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers.

Five minutes turned out to be a long time when you were forbidden from moving. Alexis sat with his feet flat on the pharmacy floor and his arm resting in the machine's cradle at roughly heart height, while Bently timed him and periodically announced "four minutes to live" in the voice of a mission control operator. Ruth asked whether his heart level was actually heart level or more of an esophagus situation, and they debated his anatomy until the timer went off. The machine hummed, the cuff tightened, and the number came up clearly lower than either of his earlier ones. Not dramatic, not miraculous, just lower, and ordinary, and believable.

They sat in the plastic chairs by the window and Alexis did the math out loud, sort of. His father loved salt the way other men loved sports teams. His father also had a stationary bike that served primarily as a coat rack. Alexis had spent the summer half-believing that the reading was a verdict, that the number would arrive fixed and final, a little stamp of determinism printed on your inner arm, and the morning had quietly dismantled that. The number moved. It depended on how you sat, on what you'd done in the last hour, on what you'd eaten all week. Ruth pointed out that this was either liberating or deeply annoying, since it meant you were responsible for it, and Alexis said both, probably, and Bently said "welcome to being eighteen."

Ms. Nakamura lived three doors down from the pharmacy, and as the three of them left she was coming out with her recycling, so Alexis, feeling bold, told her the whole thing, the drawer, the run, the five minutes, the lower number. She listened without interrupting, which he appreciated, and then asked him what diet and exercise had to do with it, and he said, slowly, assembling it as he spoke, that if the numbers shifted within an hour then they could shift over months too, that the reading was less a sentence and more a running commentary, and that his father's salt habit and coat-rack bike were both talking to that machine whether he listened or not. Ms. Nakamura said she'd save him the first week of the term, then, and Ruth said "he beguiled the machine into mercy, that's his whole method," and Alexis admitted the five quiet minutes did feel a bit like charming a small stubborn god.

He still didn't know what his father's actual baseline was, or whether one lower reading after sitting still meant anything at all about anyone's long-term health, and he was honest with himself about that hole in the middle of his knowledge. But that evening he cleared the bike of coats, set it facing the window, and put the cuff machine on the kitchen table where his father would see it at breakfast. Then he sat down across from the empty chair, feet flat on the floor, and waited, watching the second hand on the stove clock make its slow judicious circle.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
story:
Nicola had claimed the corner table by the window of the Bean Counter before Madison even got through the door, which was unfair, since Madison had texted first. The place smelled like burnt espresso and pumpkin, that desperate autumnal pumpkin that arrived earlier every year, and Nicola was guarding two cups with the posture of a woman defending a fort.

"You're late," Nicola said. "Your cocoa is getting a skin."

"I've been thinking about my ballot." Madison sat down hard enough to slosh her own cup. "It came in the mail yesterday. My actual ballot. My name, misspelled, on an official envelope."

"Thrilling."

"It is thrilling. It's the first one. You get one first one."

Nicola rolled her eyes, a mannerism she'd been polishing since seventh grade until it had achieved a kind of fluent, dismissive elegance, like a fencer's parry. "It's a municipal election, Madi. It's a school board and a drainage levy and a woman who wants to be county clerk."

"Democracy is not a spectator sport," Madison said, in her best imitation of Ms. Qureshi, their civics teacher, who said it so often that the whole class could perform it.

"Democracy is a drainage levy," Nicola said.

"You know what my grandfather said at dinner?" Madison leaned in. "He said when he was eighteen, he couldn't vote. Eighteen. Drafted into a whole war, no say in anything. I thought he was being grumpy, but I looked it up and it's true. They fixed it with the Twenty-Sixth Amendment. That's the one that set the voting age at eighteen."

"Congratulations on your amendment."

"In 1971. And here's the part that killed me. It was ratified in about three months. Faster than any other amendment. The whole country pulled that off before summer."

Nicola frowned into her cocoa. "That's it? That's the slowest thing America ever did quickly?"

"It took forever to get started and then went like lightning," Madison said. "Which is honestly my entire personality."

Martin arrived then, shaking rain off his jacket in a way that deliberately splashed both of them. He dropped into the third chair and stole a sip from Nicola's cup before she could slap his hand away, a ritual they performed like a courtly dance.

"Tell him," Nicola said.

Madison told him, the amendment, the war, the grandfather, the three months. Martin, who planned to study marine biology and could not go ten minutes without mentioning it, was currently obsessed with a poster over the register advertising some documentary, and he interrupted her twice to say the fish on it were pelagic, open-ocean fish, not reef fish, and that whoever designed the poster should be ashamed.

"Focus," Madison said. "The point is, young people had to fight to get enfranchised, and now the drainage levy, which affects literally the street I live on, is going to be decided by people whose average age is deceased. So you two are coming with me on Tuesday. Early voting is at the rec center."

"I'm registered in my mom's district," Martin lied, badly, because he had moved in August and everyone knew it.

"You can update your address at the counter."

"I don't have time between classes."

"You have one class. It's Tuesdays."

"Fine," Martin said finally, raising both hands. "Fine. I'll update my registration and I'll vote on the drainage. If it floods, that's on you."

Nicola sipped her cocoa with the composure of someone who had won. "See how easy that was? All that lightning, 1971 speed, and it still took you three months of friendship to move him."

Ms. Qureshi came in then, in her raincoat, and got in line behind them at the register while Madison ordered a refill. She greeted them, asked what they were plotting, and Madison announced, grandly, that she had organized her first electorate, that two formerly unregistered citizens would be voting Tuesday.

"Wonderful," Ms. Qureshi said. "I'll look for you there."

She paid for her coffee, and as she turned to go she mentioned, almost apologetically, that the deadline to update a registration had actually been the previous Friday, and that Martin would have to sort out a provisional ballot, which would take longer and require a form, and possibly a second trip.

Martin smiled at Madison with enormous, serene sweetness.

"About three months," he said, "should do it."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Migration can reshape a pyramid: some Gulf states, such as Qatar, show a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers live there.
story:
Jonathan had the kitchen table to himself, which meant the laptop, the textbook, two mugs of cold tea, and a printout of population pyramids were arranged in a kingdom of one. The assignment was due at eight the next morning, and Mr. Pham had been specific: choose two countries, analyse the shape of their pyramids, and argue whether each would need to build more schools or more nursing homes over the next thirty years. Jonathan had chosen Japan, which was easy, a tapering top like a squeezed balloon. The second country he had picked almost at random from the folder of charts, and now he sat staring at it, certain there had been a printing error.

The pyramid for Qatar was wrong. It had to be. Every pyramid he had seen so far curved smoothly, wide at the bottom or wide in the middle, but this one had a strange protrusion on one side, a bulge in the male bars between roughly twenty and fifty, so lopsided the chart looked bruised. He measured the bars with his pencil, wondering whether the female side had failed to print. He checked the page number, then the source line at the bottom, then the page number again.

He called Kellan, who answered with his mouth full. "You're doing Pham's thing too?"

"I think my chart's broken," Jonathan said, and held the printout up to the camera. "Look. The men's side sticks out. It's like half a pyramid."

Kellan leaned closer, chewing slower. "That's not broken. My cousin works at the airport in Doha, and she showed me a chart like that. Some Gulf states, Qatar and places like it, show a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers live there."

Jonathan lowered the page. "Foreign workers. So those aren't residents having babies."

"That's all I know. I don't know the numbers. Don't put numbers in unless you check them."

They hung up, and Jonathan sat with his hands flat on the table, annoyed with himself. He had been about to write a whole paragraph about a data error, and Mr. Pham would have marked it, and the mistake would have been his, not the chart's. The clock above the stove said ten forty. He opened the atlas his mother kept on the shelf under the phone books, found the Gulf, and looked at Qatar for a long moment, a small country with an outsized shape on the page, which was apparently also true of its population.

Here was the problem he now could not stop thinking about. Mr. Pham wanted a prediction: schools or nursing homes. For Japan the logic felt solid, a wide elderly cohort moving upward, a narrow base of children, so the country would need care for the old and fewer primary classrooms. But Qatar's pyramid was not telling one story. The bulge of working-age men was not the same thing as a generation being born; it was people arriving, and people who arrived could leave, and Jonathan did not know whether the chart was showing him the future or only the present wearing a costume. If he treated the bulge like an age cohort, he would predict nursing homes for men who might be gone by then. If he treated it as temporary, he had almost nothing to predict from at all.

He tried to verbalize the difficulty out loud, partly to hear whether it made sense, partly because the house was too quiet. "The shape shows people, but it doesn't show whether they stay," he said to the kitchen. It sounded thinner spoken than it did in his head. He texted Amin, who was the pragmatist of the three of them and would tell him to just pick an answer and sleep.

Amin's reply came in three bubbles. "Does Pham grade for being right or for the argument?" Jonathan typed back that he didn't know. "Then write the argument. Say what you'd predict if the bulge is permanent and what you'd predict if it isn't. Say you can't tell from the chart alone." Jonathan stared at the screen. It felt like a dodge, but it also felt true, and he could not find the line between those two things.

He wrote both paragraphs anyway. For the first, he reasoned as though the working-age men were a lasting feature: the country would eventually need services for them as they aged, though not schools, since the chart showed no wide base of children. For the second, he reasoned as though they were not: then the pyramid said little about the future at all, and planning would depend on choices the chart could not show him. Between the paragraphs he wrote a single sentence acknowledging that he could not decide which reading was correct from the data he had. He read it four times, worried it looked lazy, then left it, because he could not honestly write anything else.

By one in the morning the essay was saved and the pyramids were stacked in a folder, Qatar's crooked shape on top. He was too tired to be blase about it, which surprised him; he had expected the whole thing to be busywork, and instead he was lying in bed still turning the chart over in his mind. Through his wall he could hear his father's radio, tuned to the news, some announcer reading figures about a part of the world Jonathan had never thought about before tonight. He listened until the signal faded between stations, and then he got up and turned the folder over, so that Japan, with its smooth and ordinary curve, faced the ceiling instead.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1, so the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared.
story:
The kitchen smelled of cardamom because Dadi was boiling tea for the third time that afternoon, having forgotten the first two. Layla spread her books across the table anyway, claiming territory the way she had every June since she was small, and pulled out her phone to look at the photographs Aleena had sent at midnight: six derivative problems, solved in Aleena's round, hurried handwriting, due to be submitted online before the exam on Monday.

She had told Aleena she would "glance" at them. What she had not told Aleena, or anyone, was that she had spent the whole train ride here rehearsing a small, satisfying speech about how some people thought calculus was beneath checking over.

The house helped her think, that was the truth of it. At home her desk faced a wall and a poster of a tropical beach she no longer saw. Here the window gave onto the neem tree and the lane where the vegetable seller called out prices all morning, and the noise arrived as rhythm rather than demand. Dadi moved through the kitchen without comment, adjusting the flame, and Layla bent over the first photograph with the particular acumen of someone who wants to find a mistake more than she wants the work to be right.

She found it in problem one, and then again in problem two, and by problem four her pencil was ticking the margins so hard it tore the paper she was working on. The derivative of x cubed, Aleena had written, was 3x cubed. She had done the same thing everywhere: multiplied by the power and then left the power alone, never lowering it by one. Layla sat back. Last summer, before the exam that had decided their class rankings, Aleena had sat across from her at this very table and copied Layla's method off the page, saying it was faster, saying why did the exponent matter if you'd already used it. Layla had laughed and not corrected her, because the method had still produced answers close enough to pass, and because it had felt good to be the one laughing.

Now the exam was a real one, the one that counted, and the method had calcified into six wrong answers. Layla wrote out the correction on a napkin, then a proper page. The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1, she wrote, so the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared, not 3x cubed. She checked it against her textbook, twice, the way she checked anything she was about to be smug about. Then she photographed her page and typed a message that began, Aleena, before you submit, look at your powers.

Dadi set a cup of tea down beside her elbow and stayed, drying her hands on her dupatta, watching the way she watched everything, as if she understood more than she said. Layla covered the phone with her palm out of old habit, secrecy being the one skill she had truly mastered in this house.

The reply took eleven minutes. Layla read it standing at the window, where the light was going amber over the lane and the vegetable seller was packing up his unsold tomatoes. She read it a second time to be sure.

I already fixed them, Aleena wrote. I was up till two. I checked everything against the notes you lent me last week, your blue notebook, the one you said was your best work. It's all over my kitchen table. I was going to text you this morning.

Layla looked down at the napkin, at her careful page, at the turgid little paragraph she had drafted in her head on the train, all that eloquence prepared for an audience that had already left the theatre. She scrolled up to the photographs Aleena had sent, then back, and noticed for the first time the timestamp in the corner of each one, well before midnight, hours before she had even opened them. Dadi refilled her own cup and said, in a voice that suggested nothing and knew everything, "More tea, or are you finished?"

Layla picked up her pencil and turned to a fresh page.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced the five stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance in her 1969 book On Death and Dying, originally to describe terminally ill patients facing their own death.
story:
The vending machine on the fourth floor took Jesse's dollar and gave him nothing, which felt about right for the day. His grandfather had died at 6:40 in the morning, before the snow on the parking lot had even melted, and Jesse had been sitting in this corridor since eight, refusing the coffee his mother offered and the granola bar Dario's mother packed. He kicked the machine once, then again, until a nurse passing with a chart gave him a look he understood as an injunction against kicking hospital property, so he stopped.

"He was ninety-one," Dario said from the bench behind him. "That's not even sad, statistically." Dario talked like this when he didn't know what to do, turning everything into numbers, and usually it made Jesse laugh. Today it made him want to break something small, like the vending machine's glass.

"You don't get it. I don't feel anything." Jesse said it quietly, because his mother was down the hall and grief was supposed to be loud, or at least visible, and instead there was just this flat gray quiet in him, like a TV tuned to no channel. "The counselor gave us a handout in tenth grade. The five stages. Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. I keep checking, like a checklist, and I'm not on any of them. Am I broken?"

Mr. Fischer, who taught world history and coached the debate team, was in the family waiting room when Jesse went in to find the bathroom and instead sat down. Mr. Fischer's wife had been on the fourth floor since Tuesday, which was why he was there, and he had a styrofoam cup of terrible coffee and the kind of tired face that made honesty easier. Jesse asked him about the stages, mostly to fill the air, and was surprised when Mr. Fischer frowned.

"You know where those came from?" He didn't wait for an answer. "Kübler-Ross. 1969, a book called On Death and Dying. She was writing about terminally ill patients facing their own deaths. Not mourners. Everybody gets that backwards." He turned the cup in his hands. "Doesn't mean it can't apply to you. Just means nobody's grading you against it."

Jesse sat with that. The stages had felt like an assignment with a rubric, and now the rubric turned out to be for a different class entirely. Somewhere in him, something loosened, though he still couldn't name what he felt, and he was starting to think that was allowed, that the unnamed thing might be its own stage, or no stage, or just the ordinary texture of loving a person who used to sneak him licorice and enthralled him, at age six, with card tricks he later figured out were terrible. That was the part nobody's handout covered: the dead keep enthralling you after they're gone, from memory instead of a kitchen chair.

Down the hall, his grandfather's room was being packed up.
