An ancillary staff member with a laundry cart had already taken the bedding, and the bed was stripped to a plastic mattress, and this, more than the morning phone call, was what finally did it. Not the stages. The stripped bed. Jesse stood in the doorway and cried hard and briefly, like weather passing, while Dario hovered behind him holding, for some reason, a get-well card he'd never gotten to give, because he'd planned to visit next week and next week had arrived early and empty.

"I changed my mind," Dario said afterward, in the corridor, when Jesse had washed his face. "About it not being sad." He turned the card over in his hands. "You think they'd let me leave this somewhere? Like with his stuff? I wrote a joke in it. About chess. He always beat me at chess and I need him to have the joke before the stuff gets, you know, distributed." That was Dario's want, suddenly and plainly: not to be statistical, but to be remembered as someone who'd shown up.

Jesse took the card and went to find his mother, who was signing papers at the nurses' station with a pen that kept skipping. He asked, and she asked, and a nurse said family could put a card with the personal effects. So Jesse walked back down the corridor and set the envelope on the folded sweater in the plastic bag, the gray one his grandfather wore to Jesse's debate final in February, and smoothed it flat with his hand.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Aristotle named three means of persuasion: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, the logic of the argument.
story:
On the third morning in Lyon, Sophia taped her note cards to the mirror of the hotel bathroom and spoke French at her own reflection until her throat hurt. In two days she was supposed to stand in front of a classroom of French teenagers and argue, for five minutes, about whether cities should make public transit free. Her accent was decent. Her grammar held. What she had written, though, was five minutes of facts, and reading it aloud she felt the presentiment that something in it would not survive contact with an actual audience.

"You sound like a vending machine," said her brother from the doorway, in English, and she slammed the door on him.

That afternoon her host sister took her to a café where two classmates were already waiting, a boy named Kareem and a girl named Frances. They had agreed to be her practice audience. Frances pushed her coffee aside and said, "Beginne. Vas-y."

Sophia began. Free transit reduced congestion; a study in one city showed ridership rising. Free transit cut emissions. Free transit helped low-income workers. She finished in four minutes and some seconds, having used every card, and the table was quiet in a way that felt like weather.

"You had evidence," Kareem said carefully, in his lurching English, switching to help her. "But you were like a report. Nobody's heart moved. Nobody thought, this girl, I trust her."

Frances tapped the table. "In philosophy class we learned Aristotle. He named three means of persuasion. Ethos, pathos, logos." She counted them on her fingers. "Ethos, the speaker's credibility. Pathos, the audience's emotions. Logos, the logic of the argument. You brought only the last one."

Sophia looked at her cards, fanned on the table between the sugar and the ashtray, and understood that they were impermeable. Nothing warm could get in, and nothing warm could get out. Every point was a wall, and behind every wall was another wall.

Two winters ago, at her grandmother's kitchen table in Ohio, Sophia had watched her grandmother argue with an insurance adjuster on the phone for forty minutes about a claim. Her grandmother had no documents in front of her, no figures, no studies. She told the story of the pipe bursting on Christmas Eve, and how she had stood in six inches of water in her slippers, and by the end of it the adjuster's voice had changed, had gone soft and human, and the check came the next week. Twelve-year-old Sophia had thought her grandmother was just lucky. Now, in the café, she could see that her grandmother had known exactly what she was doing, that ethos and pathos were crafts you could learn, that the old woman had spent forty minutes building a person the adjuster could believe in.

"All right," Sophia said, and she turned her cards face down. "Again. In French."

She started over, slower. She talked about the woman she had seen that morning at the tram stop, counting coins in her palm while the doors closed. She admitted that free transit would cost the city money, that she didn't have all the answers, that she was a visitor arguing about someone else's home. When she stumbled on a word, she let the stumble stand instead of freezing. Kareem leaned forward. Frances had stopped checking her phone.

Afterward, walking back along the Rhône with the light going copper on the water, Sophia practiced under her breath, not the facts now but the opening she was trying to build, an opening that would preempt the room's first objection by naming it herself. Two approaches, her cards and her grandmother, and her position somewhere between them, holding both, certain of neither.

The morning of the debate, Ms. Pelletier, the teacher who had arranged the exchange, caught her in the corridor. "You have your notes?"

"I have them," Sophia said. "I might not use them."

Ms. Pelletier looked at her a moment, then held open the classroom door. Inside, thirty faces turned. Sophia walked to the front, set the cards on the desk without looking at them, and said, "Je veux vous parler d'une femme que j'ai vue hier."

Kareem, in the second row, nodded once.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
The community sports field had been converted for the afternoon into something between a stadium and a living room, folding chairs in ragged rows facing the big screen the rec department had borrowed from the high school. Taylor arrived early with her father, who carried two camp chairs and a cooler, and claimed a spot near the middle where the sound cables wouldn't trip anyone. The Olympic opening ceremony was being streamed, and half the neighbourhood had turned out for it, kids dribbling a soccer ball behind the last row, Ms. Bekele from the rec department testing the microphone she would use only once, to say welcome.

Taylor had a private project for the day. Her mother was from a country whose flag was green, yellow and red; her father's flag was blue, white and orange; and at school she had been telling people for a week that the Olympic rings contained the colors of every flag on earth, a claim she had picked up somewhere and never checked. She wanted it to be true. If it was true, then the rings on the screen were, in some quiet way, hers twice over, and the argument she kept having with herself about which box to tick on forms that asked for one background could be preempted by a symbol that refused to choose.

Kayne and Rose-Marie showed up before the ceremony started, Kayne carrying a bag of chips he guarded like contraband and Rose-Marie with a printed flag of her own country taped to a stick. They sat down on either side of Taylor, and Kayne immediately began narrating the athletes' outfits, doing a bad French accent, until Rose-Marie elbowed him into something closer to silence.

"Look at the rings," Taylor said, pointing at the screen, where the ceremony had paused on an aerial shot of the stadium. "Every color of every flag. That's the whole point of them."

"Every flag?" Kayne said. "Every single one?"

"Every single one," Taylor said, though she heard the small falseness in her voice, the way you hear a floorboard shift under your own weight.

Rose-Marie held up her little flag and began checking it against the frozen image, blue, yellow, red, a methodical girl even at parties. "Mine works," she announced. "All three."

Kayne, naturally, made it a game. He started naming flags and demanding verification. Japan, white and red, fine. Brazil, green and yellow, fine, but there was blue in the globe and Taylor said so before he could pounce. Then he said Portugal, red and green, and Taylor hesitated, because neither of those was a ring color, and the black ring suddenly looked like a stranger. She laughed it off, said she'd look it up, and did not look it up, because the phone was in her father's cooler bag and the moment was moving on.

Her father, overhearing, leaned in from the next chair. "The rings are about unity, Tay. That's what matters. Not a checklist." He said it the way he said most things, warmly and as though the conversation were already over. It was his way of thinking: symbols were affective, they worked on you from a distance, and picking them apart was missing the point. Kayne, Taylor knew, thought the opposite, that anything you believed should survive being checked, or you should stop believing it. Both positions seemed true to her in the moment and neither seemed sufficient, and she sat with that discomfort while the parade of athletes began.

She did get the phone, eventually, using the pretense of photographing Rose-Marie's flag, a small subterfuge that fooled nobody, and looked it up with the screen tilted away from the sun. What she found rearranged the afternoon. The rings had been designed in 1913 by a French baron, Pierre de Coubertin, and he had chosen the colors deliberately, so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them. She read it twice. Every national flag of the time. And there, in the same paragraph, was the part that undid her whole argument in the most satisfying way: the white background counted too.

"Kayne," she said, and waited until he lowered his commentary. "Portugal. The rings don't have red or green. But the flag has white in the shield. And the white background of the rings counts, that's part of the design, it's one of the colors."

"So my flag's color is, what, the empty part?"

"Every flag of the time," Taylor said. "Designed in 1913, by a guy named Coubertin. He picked the colors so that at least one would be in every flag, and the white background is included."

Rose-Marie considered this with her flag still in her hand. "So mine is in the yellow and red and blue. Yours is in the green and the white. Kayne's is in the black."

"Mine's the orange and white," her father said from the next chair, having apparently been listening the whole time. He said it lightly, but Taylor noticed he had abandoned his unity speech, that he was now playing the checklist game too, and that the two ways of thinking had folded into each other without anyone conceding anything.

The ceremony moved on, fireworks over the stadium mirrored, faintly, in the windows of the apartments beyond the field, and Taylor found she was less sure than before, not more, though the uncertainty felt different. The rings held every flag from 1913, but 1913 was not now, and she didn't know what happened to the claim when new countries arrived, and she didn't ask, because she suspected the answer would be another afternoon of checking. What she had was a rule that was true once and mostly true now and beautiful either way, and a father who cared about the feeling of it and a friend who cared about the facts of it, and she sat between them with both.

When the torch finally reached the top of the stadium, the whole field stood up without being asked, kids on shoulders, Ms. Bekele on her folding chair, the soccer ball abandoned in the grass. Rose-Marie raised her little flag higher, and Taylor, without deciding to, raised the phone with the five rings still on the screen, and held it there against the darkening sky.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea lost a fishing industry that had employed about 40,000 people.
story:
Olivia arrived at the community garden before anyone else, mostly to avoid her mother, who had spent the whole week rehearsing the phrase "responsible summer" as if saying it enough times would make it true. The garden occupied a scraped lot behind the laundromat, forty plots of fencing and tomato stakes, and it had a waiting list three years long, which was the only reason Olivia's application essay mattered. Ms. Warsame, who ran it, had told her the committee wanted to see "engagement." Olivia had written three hundred words about engagement and suspected every one of them was circumlocution, a fence of words around the simple fact that she wanted a plot because she was tired of the apartment, the parking lot, the whole gray geometry of her days.

Patience was already there, actually, crouched over the communal herb bed, which corrected Olivia's sense of priority immediately. "You're early," Patience said, without looking up.

"I'm avoiding my house."

"Cool. Hold this." Patience handed her a trowel and kept pinching off bolted cilantro, which had gone to flower because nobody had harvested it. "Karl's coming at ten with his thing about the water bill."

Karl's thing turned out to be the water bill. The garden's metered rate had jumped, the city was repricing usage after the reservoir dropped two feet, and Ms. Warsame had called a meeting of plot holders at the picnic table under the mulberry. Karl arrived on a bike with a folder of printouts, which he distributed like a man running for office. "If they raise the rate," he said, "half these plots go fallow. Mrs. Otero already said she can't do it."

"Then we do a shared fund," Patience said. "The people with money cover the people without."

"That's charity," Karl said. "Charity dries up."

"Being poor dries up faster."

Ms. Warsame rapped the table once. "One at a time. Olivia, you've been quiet, which is rare and suspicious."

Olivia had been quiet because she was reading Karl's printout, which was not about the reservoir at all. Page three was a case study from his geography elective, photocopied crooked, about the Aral Sea. She read it twice. "This says the Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea lost a fishing industry that had employed about 40,000 people." She looked up. "Forty thousand."

"It's famous," Karl said. "It's like the textbook example."

"So the cotton farmers got water," Olivia said slowly, "and the fishermen got a desert. And it wasn't weather. It was a decision. Somebody chose which side of the pipe to stand on." She tapped the page. "That's the water bill. That's us, at the dumbest possible scale. When the reservoir drops, the price rises, and the price doesn't fall on everybody equally. It lands on Mrs. Otero, because she's downstream of money instead of downstream of a river."

Patience pointed at her. "See, that's the fund argument."

"Sort of," Olivia said, though she could feel the argument bending in her hands. "But Karl's right that a fund is a patch. The actual system is that water gets priced like it's private and used like it's shared, and nobody upstream of the decision ever sees the downstream." She paused. "I don't know the fix. I know the shape of the break."

"You sound sagacious," Karl said. "I hate it."

"You sound like a folder," Olivia said, and even Ms. Warsame laughed into her coffee.

The meeting ended without a vote, because the committee had not actually raised the rate yet, only floated it, which Ms. Warsame called "governance by weather balloon." People drifted back to their plots. Olivia took the printout home, read the rest of the case study on the bus, and read it again in the kitchen while her mother asked whether she had thought more about a real job. She had not. She was thinking about Mrs. Otero's tomatoes, which would die not from drought but from arithmetic.

The twist came on Thursday. Olivia stopped by the laundromat to drop off the folder Karl had left in her bag and found Mrs. Otero at the counter, feeding quarters into a dryer she did not need, because the machine's exhaust vented warm air and her apartment ran cold and the utility rate had gone up too. "Everything rises together," Mrs. Otero said, cheerful in a way that eviscerated Olivia a little, the way a person can be cheerful about being cornered. "Water, gas, bread. You young people plot your vegetables. In my day we plotted revolutions." She laughed at her own joke and pulled the last warm towel out.

Olivia stood there holding the folder, understanding something she could not yet say cleanly: that the garden was not separate from the laundromat, that Karl's bill and Mrs. Otero's dryer and a dried-up sea on another continent were all one machine with many dials, and that she had spent her essay talking about engagement as if caring were a hobby. She walked back to the lot, past the fence, and found Patience and Karl arguing at the herb bed over whether to rip out the bolted cilantro or let it reseed for free.

"Let it reseed," Olivia said. "Free water, free seed. Then we take the fund idea to Ms. Warsame, and we make the fund buy a rain barrel."

Karl squinted. "A rain barrel won't fix a reservoir."

"No," Olivia said. "But it keeps Mrs. Otero's plot alive while we figure out what will." She knelt down beside the cilantro, which had gone lanky and stubborn and was flowering anyway, and began to weed around it, her hands in the dirt, the flowers leaning toward whatever sun the mulberry left them.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A simple random sample of about 1,000 people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3 percentage points for the whole sample's results.
story:
Elliot had the printout flat on Ms. Traoré's desk before the bell finished ringing, one finger holding down the corner as though the paper might bolt. "Six hundred and twelve respondents," he said. "It's the survey. The one I told you about. Simeon wants to run it Thursday with the number in the headline."

Ms. Traoré looked at the page but kept her hands in her lap. "And you want my permission, or my blessing?"

"Neither. I want to know if it's right." He had known her for three years, since algebra, and he knew the difference between her silences. This was the silence that meant she was waiting for him to answer his own question. He straightened up anyway and waited it out.

The survey was real. The student newspaper had emailed it to every family on the district list, and six hundred and twelve people had answered the question about later start times for the high school. Fifty-three percent said yes. Simeon, who was co-editor, had written the headline already: MAJORITY OF FAMILIES BACK LATER START. He had shown it to Elliot at lunch with the particular confidence of someone holding a proof, and Cayden had leaned across the table and said, "Six hundred people out of how many? The district has like four thousand families. Isn't that basically nothing?" Simeon had waved him off. "It's more than professional polls use." Elliot had said nothing, which was unusual for him, and had spent the afternoon feeling like he'd swallowed a stone.

At lunch the next day, Cayden brought his laptop to the table and turned it so the others could see. "Okay, so I looked it up. A simple random sample of about a thousand people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus three percentage points." He said it flatly, reading. "For the whole sample's results."

"Margin of error," Simeon repeated, the way he repeated things he intended to dismiss.

"It's the wiggle room," Cayden said. "How much the number could be off by." He scrolled. "But here's the thing. Ours wasn't random. It was whoever opened the email."

Elliot took a bite of his sandwich and chewed slowly. The cafeteria smelled like bleach and hamburger grease; a sophomore at the next table was trying to balance a milk carton on its edge. "So the thousand thing doesn't even apply," he said finally. "That's for a simple random sample. Everyone has the same chance of being picked."

"Which we don't have," said Cayden.

"Right. But it's still the only number we know." Elliot pulled the printout from his binder, the same one he'd shown Ms. Traoré, and turned it over to the blank side. He wrote 53 at the top. Below it, out to either side, he wrote 50 and 56. "If a thousand people would give us plus or minus three, and we have six hundred, the honest wiggle room is even bigger than that. And on top of that, who answers a school email? My mom answers school emails. She'd answer that survey four times if it let her." He tapped the 50. "Fifty-three could be half. It could be under half."

Simeon leaned back with his arms crossed. The vitriolic tone that had won him two arguments at the editorial board meeting last month was in his voice when he said, "So we just don't report anything. We have six hundred people telling us something and we sit on it because of your mom." His milieu, Elliot thought, was exactly this: a cafeteria table converted into a courtroom, with Cayden as the jury and Elliot as whoever was losing. But that wasn't fair, and Elliot made himself pull the thought back. Simeon wasn't wrong to want the paper to matter. The paper had spent two years abrogating its own authority, running mood-board content and horoscopes, and this survey was the first real thing it had produced.

"That's not what I'm saying," Elliot said. "We report it. We just don't say 'majority.' We say what it is. Six hundred and twelve respondents, fifty-three percent, and we say the method, that it was whoever answered an email. Then people can decide." He looked at the numbers on the back of the printout. "If we had a thousand, randomly picked, we'd get plus or minus three, and even then fifty-three would only mean probably more than half. We're way past the point where a headline is honest."

Cayden pulled the laptop back toward himself. "There's a stats teacher here. Mr. Something. He posts the response rates for his own polls on his door."

Simeon was quiet for a moment, working a tater tot apart with his thumb. "Fifty-three," he said. "It's a good number. It feels true."

"That's the problem," Elliot said. He capped his pen.

Thursday was still two days away. Simeon took the printout from the table, folded it once, and put it in his back pocket without agreeing to anything. Then he stood, gathered his tray, and walked toward the drop-off window, and Cayden closed the laptop and watched him go.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: The 1967 Holmes and Rahe stress scale lists a change in residence as a stressful life event worth 20 points, the same as a change in schools.
story:
The truck's passenger seat had a crack running through it, and Alexia kept her thumb pressed into the vinyl as the highway markers slid past. Her father drove with both hands on the wheel, saying nothing, which was its own kind of conversation. Behind them, in the box, were forty boxes and her mattress and a bicycle she hadn't ridden in a year. Two hundred and thirty miles behind them, or nearly, were Teegan and Kade and the parking lot where they'd all sat on Kade's hood the night before, until the streetlight clicked off and nobody moved for a while.

She had expected to feel something large. What she felt instead was a small, persistent tiredness, the kind that made her blink too slowly, and it annoyed her, because nothing had actually happened to her. Nobody had died. She wasn't sick. Her father had a job offer, and they had packed, and here they were. "I don't get why I'm so wiped," she said to the windshield. Her father glanced over. "It's a lot," he offered, and she thought that was too easy an answer, so she took out her phone.

Teegan had sent her a photograph an hour ago: the stress scale from some psychology thing, screenshotted from a website with a gray background and clip-art borders, the kind of site that looked like it hadn't been updated since Alexia was in kindergarten, almost obsolescent. She scrolled down the list, waiting for the numbers to load in chunks. Marriage, 50 points. Divorce, 50. She kept scrolling, curious now despite herself, the way she got when a system was involved, some hidden arithmetic underneath a feeling.

There it was. A change in residence, 20 points. She read the line twice, then looked at the entry just below it, because the numbers matched, and she sat forward against the seatbelt. A change in schools, also 20. The same. She'd been telling herself all summer that the school part was the hard part, the real part, and that the house, the town, the move itself was just logistics, boxes and a rental truck. But the scale counted them equally, as if leaving a bedroom and leaving a hallway were the same weight of event. And she was doing both at once, which meant, if the arithmetic meant anything, she was carrying forty points of it before the summer had even properly ended.

"Teegan found something," she said, and turned the phone toward her father at a red light. He squinted at it. "Holmes and Rahe," she said. "1967. Psychologists. They made a scale of stressful life events and gave each one points." He read for a moment, then said, "Huh," which from him was a speech. "Twenty for moving," she said. "Same as changing schools. Exactly the same." He pulled forward as the light changed. "So it's not just me being dramatic." He said it gently, not as a question, and she didn't answer, because she was already wondering about the other side of it, whether a thing being countable made it smaller or larger.

Because here was what she couldn't decide. Part of her wanted the number to be an excuse, a permission slip: the scale said so, therefore the exhaustion was legitimate, therefore she could lie down in this truck and be tired without rectitude or self-judgment, without the little prosecutor in her head asking what exactly you've done to earn this fatigue. But another part of her suspected that weighing a thing was a way of putting it down, of filing it. Her grandmother's death was 63 points on that list, and a move was 20, and she trusted the difference between those, and yet she didn't quite trust that grief could sit on the same ruler as a truck full of boxes. Both ideas seemed true. She held them the way you hold two groceries in one hand.

They stopped for gas outside a town whose water tower she could see from the pump. Her father went inside to pay, and Alexia walked around the box of the truck, pressing her palm flat against the sun-warmed metal, listening to the tick of the engine cooling. Kade called while she stood there. "Did you see what Teegan sent?" he said. "I saw it. Twenty points. Same as a new school." There was a pause with road noise in it, his road or hers, she couldn't tell. "Does that make you feel better or worse?" he asked, and she laughed, because he'd landed on the exact question, as he tended to.

"Both," she said. "It makes me feel both." She told him the thing about the prosecutor in her head, and he said he had one of those too, though his mostly showed up during exams. She asked him whether he thought you could count a feeling without shrinking it, and he said he had no idea, but that it was a good question, and she liked that he didn't pretend otherwise. A hawk crossed over the water tower, unhurried. "Text me when you get there," he said. "I will. Teegan too." "Obviously Teegan too," he said, and she smiled at the blank side of the truck.

Her father came back with two bottles of water and a bag of gas-station candy she hadn't asked for, which was his way of saying things. They climbed in. The seat crack was still there, and she put her thumb in it again, an old habit already, four hours old. Somewhere ahead was a town she'd never acclimated to, a school that counted the same as everything in this truck, a bedroom that would smell like somebody else's paint for a while. She didn't know yet which idea she'd keep, the permission slip or the suspicion of it, and she found she could stand not knowing, for at least the length of one more highway.

"Twenty points," her father said suddenly, pulling back onto the road, as if he'd been doing the math the whole time. "And school's another twenty." She looked at him. "So I'm at forty," she said. He nodded at the mirrors, checking the merge, and said, "Buckle up for the rest."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel.
story:
The metronome stood on the corner of the piano like a small wooden sentry, its brass pendulum frozen mid-arc. Riley had noticed it on his first evening at his grandfather's house, three days into what his mother kept calling a sabbatical, though it was really just the summer between high school and everything after. His grandfather had left the piano to him for the season, along with a beginner's book and one instruction: play something by August.

He could not play anything by August. He could play the first eight bars of a waltz, badly, and he could find middle C without looking, which felt like less of an accomplishment every day. His grandfather sat in the next room with the radio on, pretending not to listen, and Riley pretended not to hear him pretending.

"You're rushing," his grandfather called through the doorway on the fourth day. "Every time. You start slow and then you run away from yourself."

Riley lifted his hands off the keys. He reached over and set the metronome going, and the room filled with its dry, patient tick. "Who even invented this thing?" he asked, half to the room, half to the doorway.

His grandfather came in, wiping his hands on a dish towel, and looked at the little machine the way you look at someone you've known a long time. "Johann Maelzel patented it in 1815," he said. "Though the design wasn't really his. He drew on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel." He tapped the wooden case once. "Winkel got the idea and Maelzel got the patent. Decide for yourself which one mattered."

Riley thought about that while he practiced, the tick dividing the afternoon into equal pieces. At home he had learned everything the opposite way: fast, loose, by feel. His friend Jaeden played guitar like that, all instinct and swagger, and Riley had always envied it, the way Jaeden could pick up an instrument at a party and enthrall a whole room without seeming to try. Riley had once recorded himself playing the waltz and sent it to Jenna, who texted back "it's cute that you're doing this," a sentence he had read maybe forty times.

He worked at the metronome anyway. Sixty beats a minute, then sixty-four, the numbers marked on the plate in small stamped figures. When he matched it, the music sounded mechanical. When he ignored it, it fell apart. He began to suspect the machine was a kind of trick, that the point wasn't the tick itself but the argument it forced him to have with his own hands, and he kept losing that argument.

On the sixth day he got angry at it. He pushed the sliding weight up the pendulum, let it fly, and played as fast as he could, wild and crashing, until his grandfather appeared in the doorway with an expression Riley couldn't read. "That sounded vitriolic," his grandfather said. "The piano didn't do anything to you." Riley laughed before he meant to, and the anger went out of him the way air goes out of a cushion, all at once and without dignity.

That evening Jenna and Jaeden drove out to visit, and Riley showed them the metronome because it was the most interesting thing in the house. Jaeden picked it up, set the weight somewhere arbitrary, and let it clatter. "It's a cage," he said. "Music shouldn't be a cage." Jenna turned the case over in her hands, read the faded label, and set it back exactly where it had been. "Winkel invented it and Maelzel took it," she said. "That's the actual cage." Riley looked at the two of them, then at the piano, and understood that he agreed with both of them and couldn't say why that didn't feel like a contradiction.

After they left he played the waltz once more, slowly, with the metronome ticking beside him. Partway through he stopped watching the pendulum and just listened, and for eight bars, maybe ten, his hands and the machine arrived at the same place at the same time, neither one leading. Then he lost it, and the ticking went on without him, patient as ever, and he set his fingers back at the beginning.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Under the US Credit CARD Act of 2009, card statements must show how long it would take to pay off the balance by making only the minimum payment.
story:
Natalie had chosen the bank on Delmore Street because it was empty at four in the afternoon, and she wanted a counter to herself. She carried two things in her backpack: a bank envelope with four hundred dollars in birthday and graduation money, and her first credit card statement, which had arrived on Saturday and which she had read three times on her bed with a growing sense that she had missed something.

At the teller window she deposited the cash into a savings account she had opened online two weeks before. The teller, a man with reading glasses pushed up into his hair, pointed at a small printed slip. "Your rate is variable," he said. "It changes, but right now it's four point one five percent. Left alone, the money grows." Natalie nodded and folded the slip into her wallet, next to the statement she had not yet mentioned.

She found Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya at the desk nearest the window. He had been her neighbour for eleven years before he retired from the bank, and he still came in on Tuesdays to help people with paperwork, a folding sign on his desk that read GENERAL QUESTIONS. She sat down across from him and unfolded the statement on the blotter.

"I bought a laptop," she said. "Six hundred forty dollars. Books too. I start at Fairhaven in the fall and my mom's hours got cut." She turned the page toward him and put her finger under a box in the fine print, below the payment table. "This part. It says if I make only the minimum payment, it'll take me some number of years to pay it off. I counted the number twice. Is that real?"

Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya read the box, then turned the paper around so it faced her again. "That's the law," he said. "Under the CARD Act, statements have to tell you that. How long it takes if you only pay the minimum." He did not say more. He slid the statement back and waited, which was his way.

She counted on her fingers, though the box had already done the arithmetic for her. The laptop, which she had thought of as six hundred forty dollars, would cost more than that, and the years in the box were years she would still be paying for a machine she might have replaced by then. Meanwhile the four hundred across the lobby, doing nothing, would sit and grow at four point one five percent, small numbers becoming slightly less small, without her touching it. Money you owed worked against you over time; money you held worked for you. She had never had both facts in front of her on the same afternoon.

Kirsten arrived at five, shaking rain off her jacket, because they had planned to walk to the bus stop together. She dropped into the chair beside Natalie and read the statement upside down. "Just pay the minimum," she said. "Everyone does. Charles-Olivier's been doing it for a year on his card and he's fine." Then she squinted at the box, righted the page in Natalie's hands, and stopped talking.

"Charles-Olivier is a neophyte who thinks interest is something that happens to other people," Natalie said. "He was facetious about my deposit this morning. He said watching savings grow is like watching paint dry, and I should subsume my budget under one word, fun." She looked at the box again. The paint did dry slowly. That was the point of it. But the years in the box were also slow, and they were slow in the other direction, and she had assumed until this afternoon that the two things were the same thing. They were not.

Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya asked whether she wanted to set up an automatic payment above the minimum. She said she did, and he turned his keyboard toward her and showed her the screen where she could choose the amount. Kirsten leaned over her shoulder. Natalie typed a number, deleted it, typed a larger one, and paused with her finger above the enter key.

"Mom gets paid Friday," she said to Kirsten. "I'll ask her before I do this. If she can cover half this month, I can pay more than I thought."

"Text her now," Kirsten said.

Natalie pulled out her phone, typed "can you help with the card this month, I'll explain at dinner," and pressed send.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
story:
Kayla's father had cleared the coffee table of everything except the dip bowl, which meant he was serious. By six o'clock the living room held her parents, her uncle, Eliott sprawled on the rug with his phone, and Charles-Edouard, who had never watched a full soccer match in his life and kept asking questions at the exact moment someone was about to shoot. The semi-final started at seven, and the house rule, unwritten but iron, was that nobody spoke during the anthem.

"There's more teams this year, isn't there?" Charles-Edouard said, wedging chips into the dip like a man testing its solvency, as if the bowl might declare bankruptcy. "Eliott says forty-eight. That can't be right."

"It's right," Eliott said without looking up. "Forty-eight. First time ever."

Her uncle snorted from the armchair. "First time for a lot of things this year. Three countries hosting. Never been done. Canada, Mexico, us. You kids realize this is historic?"

"You've said that four times," Kayla said.

"Because it's true four times."

She let it go and went to the kitchen for ice, and that was where her mother cornered her, or seemed to; her mother never actually cornered anyone, she just stood where you were already going. "Your grandmother's not coming," she said quietly. "Your father hasn't mentioned it. Don't bring it up before the match."

Kayla had suspected as much. Gran had promised to come for the semi-final weeks ago, had talked about it on the phone with the specific enthusiasm she reserved for things she wasn't sure she could do. Her knee had been bad since spring, the kind of pain that didn't debilitate exactly, but made stairs a negotiation. Kayla carried the ice back in and sat on the floor beside Eliott, holding the new knowledge like a stone in her cheek.

The pregame show was doing a montage of the three host cities, drone shots of stadiums, and Charles-Edouard leaned forward. "So it's the first World Cup with forty-eight teams and the first with three countries hosting," he recited, as if memorizing it for later. "Is that in the rules now? Forty-eight forever?"

"Nothing's forever," Eliott's mother's boyfriend had apparently told him, because Eliott quoted people nobody in the room knew. "FIFA changes things when it suits them."

"It suits the small countries," the uncle said. "More teams, more chances. Cape Verde qualified this year. You know what that means to a country that size?"

"It means the group stage is bloated," Kayla's father said, his first complete sentence since kickoff approached. "It dilutes the tournament. An anachronistic purist like me remembers when sixteen teams meant every match mattered."

"Every match still matters," Charles-Edouard said.

"You've watched four matches in your life."

"Four very good ones."

Kayla watched her father, not the screen. He was checking his phone in the dark, the glow climbing his face, and she could see it was Gran, a message about her knee and the stairs and maybe next time. He put the phone face down on his knee and did not say anything, and when the whistle blew he stood up like a man answering a summons.

The first half was tense and low on goals, which suited nobody's nerves. At halftime her mother brought out the tray of sandwiches and her father disappeared into the garage, and Eliott nudged Kayla's shoulder. "Your dad okay?"

"Gran's not coming," Kayla said. "Don't say anything."

"I wasn't going to."

"I know. I just needed to say it out loud once, to somebody under fifty."

She sat with it through the second half. She understood her father's version of the game, the small perfect tournament where scarcity made everything precious, because it was the same instinct that made him scrub the coffee table before guests arrived, that made him keep a landline he never used. But she understood the uncle too, and even Charles-Edouard, memorizing the numbers of the thing like a password to a larger world. Forty-eight teams meant someone's tiny country in the montage, someone's grandmother staying up past midnight. Both things were true and they rubbed against each other like the halves of the same match, and she couldn't make them agree, and maybe didn't want to. What she did know, watching her father's stillness, was that a man could love a version of a thing so much he forgot to enjoy the thing itself, and she didn't intend to do that tonight.

The goal came in the eighty-fourth minute, a scramble off a corner, and the room detonated. Her father burst back in from the garage mid-celebration, swept her mother off her feet, and for a second Kayla saw his phone on the counter where he'd left it, still face down, Gran's unread follow-up waiting. He was laughing now, shouting at the replay, entirely here. He could call after. He would call after.

"Kayla," Charles-Edouard said over the noise, "who do we want in the final?"

She picked up her father's phone and held it out to him across the chaos. "Dad. Call Gran before the highlights."
